The audio files are kept for the session (`.ample/ai/clips/`), the information stays in the history. API: `GET /api/ai/tasks/{id}/clip/{clip}`.

Requests for a Flemish sound

When a request asks for music to sound more Flemish, Codex is guided to treat that as an open direction rather than a single genre or a caricature. It should follow details the user gives, avoid inventing dialect, and consider whether the request concerns Flemish Dutch wording/prosody, a local or traditional feel, contemporary Flemish music, or another quality. When the intended direction is open to interpretation, it can offer a few musically distinct short variants with ample_present, explain their differences, and let the user choose. Codex may also offer extra iterations as an option—for example, explore contrasting directions, compare them, then refine the chosen one. Extra rounds are optional and should help resolve an open direction; they are not added to narrow requests and do not guarantee a more Flemish result.

In a finished proposal, Codex's written summary is part of the scrollable Output content, below the fixed tab row, so opening Output does not shift the tabs vertically.

Assistant tab sessions

The bottom Assistant tab stores named conversations in the open project's .ample/ai/assistant-sessions/ folder. The index keeps each session title and task references; task snapshots and the bounded activity log are stored beside it. Project switching therefore loads a different session index. Create, rename and delete are available in the tab; a session with a live task or an unapplied proposal cannot be deleted.

Assistant task outcomes are also written to AMPLE Redux, including redacted request/summary metadata, proposal change counts and hashes for content-addressed before/after text, plus presented audio clip hashes and render settings. Full conversation capture is off by default. When creating a session or from its archive control, it can be enabled for new messages; an additional explicit choice can import earlier messages still available for that session. Captured text is redacted for common credential patterns before it enters Redux. Existing task-log files may contain earlier conversation text, but the Assistant view hides those messages while capture is off.

The Health page shows aggregate AMPLE Redux storage use. The default 10 GiB budget warns at one fifth (2 GiB); changing the project budget changes both thresholds proportionally. Preview compaction shows the exact segment, record, summary and byte impact; compaction then requires a separate confirmation. Records are never pruned automatically.

Starting from the tab opens the same full prompt and proposal interface as other Codex entry points. The task keeps the session ID, while existing task APIs remain usable; callers that omit it receive an automatically named session. The session list opens its newest task and exposes earlier requests in the same conversation.

Codex threads are started as persistent app-server threads. After a server restart, the task snapshot and temporary project copy are retained. The task appears as interrupted and offers Resume conversation, which reconnects with thread/resume and registers the AMPLE MCP server at the current server URL. A task stopped with Stop now can also resume when it already has a saved thread; it reconnects to the same conversation and leaves the proposal unaccepted until you continue or accept it. Tasks cancelled before Codex starts a thread offer Ask again instead. The proposal remains unaccepted if the thread cannot be resumed. Runtime recovery still depends on Codex retaining that thread and the temporary work directory remaining available.

Accept selected & continue is available for one or more checked proposal files when the task is ready, not stale, and its complete proposal build succeeded. AMPLE validates the selected text, checkpoints the project, journals non-song writes, updates the accepted baseline, and then sends the supplied continuation instruction into the same Codex thread. Remaining files stay proposed in the temporary project. If the follow-up fails, already accepted files remain in the project and the task shows the failure; no remaining files are accepted automatically. API: GET/POST /api/ai/sessions, PATCH/DELETE /api/ai/sessions/{id}, POST /api/ai/tasks/{id}/resume, and POST /api/ai/tasks/{id}/accept-selected-continue.

Moves that Codex proposes (2026-10-10)

Codex can propose moving or renaming a project file or folder (a sample, a module, a song, a whole folder) with the tool ample_move. A move is never made in the temporary copy (it holds only the files in scope, not your audio or your other songs): it is made at Accept, after the file changes, one by one, with every path in the songs and modules that points at it following (the same refactor as Move in the project panel). Codex chooses how:

  • confirm: "ask": you get an approval card now (Codex asks to move a file or folder) and Codex waits for your answer. Approve the move records it as approved, Deny tells Codex, which goes on without it. Codex uses this when the rest of its work depends on the move. In Unsafe / Auto-all mode there is no question.
  • confirm: "propose" (the default): the move is listed under Moves Codex proposes in the proposal with a checkbox, the number of lines in your songs that will follow, and the reason. Ticked moves are made at Accept; nothing moves before.

Refused when it is proposed: a source that does not exist, a destination that exists (a move never overwrites), a folder into itself, .ample, the song of the task itself, or a path that is already part of another proposed move. A move is skipped at Accept (with a note in the log) when a song that would have to change has unsaved changes, or when the source is gone or the destination exists by then. Undo puts accepted moves back, the references following again. Accept selected (and Accept selected & continue remaining) make the approved and the ticked moves too, after the checked files; a move that is not ticked stays in the proposal.

The separate tool ample_move_file moves a text file inside the staged proposal without overwriting. Its source and destination are project-relative; workspace/<filename> can recover a misplaced text file from the working-copy root. It changes no live project file before Accept. Use ample_move for a project file or folder whose references need to follow the move.

The tool ample_copy_file (2026-10-14) copies a text file inside the staged proposal to a new, not-yet-existing path; unlike ample_move_file the source stays in place. Use it to duplicate a sequence or module before changing the copy, so other songs that still point at the original are unaffected — for example giving one song its own patched copy of a sequence that other songs also use. A workspace/<path> source instead stages a file ample_fetch_url downloaded into assets/web/ of the working folder (an image, a PDF, a fetched score) into the project, since nothing else can move a fetched asset out of the working folder and into the proposal.

ample_import_score (2026-10-15) also accepts a staged PDF or image of printed music, recognized with Audiveris (optical music recognition) when it is installed, and a MuseScore/Guitar Pro/Capella/Overture file or a zipped .mxl, converted with MuseScore (or unzipped directly for .mxl) — see docs/score-import.md. The typical flow for a score found on the web: ample_fetch_url to download it, ample_copy_file with a workspace/ source to stage it into the proposal, then ample_import_score on the staged path. OMR can misread a source, so the tool's answer says to check the note count before trusting it; a MuseScore/.mxl conversion is a faithful machine conversion, not recognition.

API: POST /api/ai/context/move (for the tool), moves: [id] (the ticked ones) on POST /api/ai/tasks/{id}/accept, accept-selected and accept-selected-continue, moves in the task JSON. ample_copy_file posts to POST /api/ai/context/copy-file.

Variants (several alternatives in one proposal)

When the request is for several alternatives of one thing (three instruments for a phrase, other beats), the model makes all of them in the one temporary copy, each as its own blocks, and calls the MCP tool ample_offer_variants once: for every variant a name, a one-line summary, the blocks that belong to it and the listen block (the end of its chain). The task then carries variants. Koda shows them as A, B and C: a variant is the proposal with only its own blocks (the changes that belong to no variant are in all of them), each can be listened to on its own (only its listen block is built, from the proposal), the block as it is now can be played to compare, and "Use this one" puts only that variant in the song as one undo step. Nothing is recognised from the words of the request: the model offers the variants through the tool.

Resuming a session after hours (2026-10-23)

A session keeps its working copy and its Codex conversation for 24 hours after its last use (a Koda question for one hour), also after Accept or Reject, as long as the copy is not bigger than 500 MB. In that time the assistant tab can resume it ("Resume conversation"): the same Codex thread is reopened in the same copy. The first turn after a resumption starts with an AMPLE NOTE: how long ago, what happened to the last proposal (accepted, rejected, undecided) and which files of the copy differ from the project now. The tool ample_changes_since lets the model look further: no arguments gives the overview, path the diff of that file (what the copy was based on against the project now), and path with import=true brings the project's version into the copy, merged with the model's own edits (a clash is reported, never guessed). Koda uses the same thread resume for Hang around, with the song brought up to date by the normal preparation.

Access outside the project: what the assistant may do and how it asks

Status (2026-10-11): built. For the assistant and for people.

The assistant (Codex) works in a copy of the project. Inside that copy and in its ./scratch folder it needs no permission. Everything else needs the person's say-so.

For the assistant

  • Remarks about AMPLE (what is missing, what could be better, how to fix it): ample_findings { text, name? }. It writes to notes/ai-findings/ inside the project. No permission needed. Say where it is in your last message.
  • A file somewhere else (a full path such as C:\temp\x.txt): first ample_request_access { path, why, minutes, kind? }. The person sees what, why and for how long, and answers allow (for that long), always for this project or deny. After an allow use ample_write_outside { path, text }. Never try another way to write there.
  • If you try anyway (a command or a file change outside the working folder) AMPLE stops the run at that request and asks the person: allow once, always for this project, or ask it to do it correctly; in the last case you are told to use ample_findings or ample_request_access.
  • What is missing: when a tool answers with a hint (a PDF reader, the voice worker, ffmpeg), tell the person and recommend the hint. ample_project_log lists them with how to fix.

For people

  • The question appears in the task window with the path, the reason and the time. Always for this project is kept in .ample/ai/grants.json and listed (with Revoke) under Projects, Health.
  • ample doctor --env checks what the tools need around the program (libraries, ffmpeg, Python, the sound font, free disk space) and writes what is missing, with how to fix it, to the project log (.ample/logs/project-log.jsonl, shown on the Health page).
  • A grant of kind passthrough only allows AMPLE's own ample_write_outside, never a direct write.
  • Never open for writing: the project's own .ample folder and the system folders.

Codes

AMP5610 (a path that can never be allowed or is not a full path), AMP5611 (no permission for that path), AMP5458 (the task is no longer running: AMPLE was restarted or the task ended; start a new task, nothing is lost in the project).

History v1: branches and promote (mock)

Status (2026-10-02): design sketch from a brainstorm. Nothing here is built or tested.

Keep it simple for now: you can branch, but you never merge content. You promote one branch to be the main line and continue from there.

Model

  • Revisions form a graph with parents[] (so multiple parents are representable, e.g. when importing from git), but the tool only creates single-parent revisions.
  • main is the main line. Other branches are experiments.
  • Promote = choose: main now points at the branch tip. No content is merged, so there are no conflicts.
  • The old main tip is kept as archive/main-<date> (read-only, can be branched from again). Nothing is deleted.
  • Sealed releases stay valid forever, also those made on an archived line; ample lineage shows them under the archive.
  • Every promote writes an entry in the hash-chained ledger: which branch, which old tip, who, when.

Commands

ample branch <name>                  # new branch from the current revision
ample branches                       # list with revisions ahead of main
ample promote <name> --dry-run       # show what changes and what drops off main
ample promote <name>                 # main -> <name>, old main tip archived
ample branch --from archive/<name> <new>   # continue an archived line

Rules for promote

  • Clean working tree; static checks (syntax, cycles, hash references) pass on the target.
  • If main has moved on since the branch point, the dry run lists the revisions and releases that drop off main (they stay in the archive).
  • Other branches stay as they are; promoting one of them later replaces main again. Never a merge.

Git mirror

Promote moves main of the mirror; the old tip is kept as a hidden ref refs/ample/archive/*, so ordinary git clients do not see branches vanish. The mirror is derived data and may be force-updated.

Listening A/B between branches (cheap, fits v1)

ample ab <branch1> <branch2> --block chorus previews the same block from both branches.

Navigating history: go, promote, peek, undo

Every revision ever made stays visible and reachable; moving around never rewrites history, only pointers move.

Two pointers

  • here (current): the revision you are on and working from.
  • the real deal (main): the revision that counts as the official one.

Double-clicking any revision moves here. "Make this the real deal" (promote) moves main. They are independent, so you can look and work without changing what is official.

Example. Go 5 revisions back (double-click, or ample go ~5). Make a commit: because you are not on a tip, it starts a new line automatically (named after the fork point, renamable; there is no loose "detached HEAD" where work can get lost, every tip stays reachable). Then change your mind: "1 back from the original line, then 5 up" is another double-click, or ample go ~1 followed by ample go +5. +N follows the path you walked before (like a browser's forward button), also through forks. In the graph: left/right along a line, up/down to switch line at a fork.

The graph (like a git client): all revisions including other lines and the archive (faded), with markers for here, the real deal, releases and bookmarks. Context menu: Go here · Look only · Make this the real deal · Fork here (name a line) · Compare with now or with the real deal · Listen A/B · Bookmark · Take just this block · Copy id. Search by block, message or release.

Commands

ample log                       # the graph: every revision, all lines (hashes shown here)
ample leaves                    # the branches/leaves from where you stand (the natural way to navigate)
ample go <line|leaf|~N|+N>      # move "here" by line name, leaf number or steps (--peek: read-only)
ample go <hash>                 # allowed, but the exception; normally you pick from `leaves`/`log`
ample promote <rev>             # move the real deal; old tip kept as archive/main-<date>
ample undo   ample redo         # step back and forth in the operation log
ample mark "before-the-remix"   # bookmark
ample purge <rev> --reason "…"  # real deletion: deliberate, logged, rare

rewind is simply go + promote; restore is not needed: a commit after go forks by itself.

Operation log (like Jujutsu's): every go and promote is recorded, so undo and redo always take you back to where you were.

Safeguards

  • Moving with unsaved work makes an automatic checkpoint (auto/...), so nothing is lost. Automatic checkpoints are also made before promote, block updates and migrations.
  • What comes back with a revision: songs and editable text sources (.amplet, lyrics, chords, .txt, .md, .csv, .json, .seq and .ampleseq), lock, cuts, baked data blocks and the modules enabled in the project. Takes stay in the shared take bank (immutable). Secrets live outside history and do not change.
  • Sealed releases stay where they are; going back never un-releases. Lineage keeps showing them.
  • A baked block is only cleaned up (ample gc) when no revision or archive refers to it.
  • Tools from back then may be missing: verify --present warns ("acestep@b7ba6d9 not available; baked data is present").
  • Revisions may also be addressed by a date (@2026-10-05) or relative (@5d), but the primary way is the revision itself.

Credentials get their own timeline

Secrets (API keys, tokens, signing key, passphrases) are not part of the project history. They live in a separate, protected store with their own timeline: every change (added, rotated, revoked, who/when) is a numbered entry, but the values are sealed (master passphrase, optional recovery key). Consequences:

  • Going back in the project history never brings back or exposes an old secret, and never overwrites the current one.
  • A revision only records which credential it needed (name and version), not the value. verify can say "needs weather_api v2, current is v3".
  • Credentials have their own log, undo (restore a rotated value) and expiry; a revoked value can be purged on its own.
  • The credential timeline is included in a backup only as sealed data, see Backup.

Purge is a dangerous act

Removing data that is no longer relevant (old takes, baked blocks, archived lines, old credential versions) must be possible, but it is the one operation in AMPLE that cannot be undone, so it is treated as dangerous:

  • Never implicit. Nothing purges as a side effect of another command; gc only removes what nothing refers to and says so, anything else needs purge.
  • Explicit acceptance. ample purge first shows a dry run: what is removed, how much space, which revisions, releases, lineage links and baked blocks lose their data, which releases would drop from data-exact to recipe-exact (or become unreproducible), and what stays untouched.
  • Backup suggestion. Before anything is deleted it says: "This cannot be undone. Make a backup first?" and offers ample backup right there (profile suggested from what is affected). Skipping needs an explicit choice.
  • Acceptance by typing, not a bare yes: the user types the scope (for example the number of revisions or the line name), or passes --accept "<what>" with a reason in scripts. A UI needs the same: a red dialog listing the impact, a backup button, and a confirm that stays disabled until the scope is typed.
  • Leaves a tombstone: the operation log keeps who, when, what scope and the reason; revisions stay in the graph as "purged (data removed)" so lineage remains understandable. Sealed releases are never purged without separate, stronger confirmation.

Navigating by leaves, not hashes

Hashes are poor handles for people, so go is aimed at lines and leaves (the tips you can actually continue from); a hash is accepted but is the exception. ample leaves shows, from where you are now, what is reachable and how far:

$ ample leaves
  here  ●  chorus-rework  (3 revisions after the split from main)
  [1]   ★  main           +2 ahead of the split   "mastered v2"            release: v2
  [2]      verse-redo     +4                      "new voice for verse"
  [3]      archive/main-2026-10-02  +1            (archived)               faded
  [4]      auto/before-promote      +0            (automatic checkpoint)
$ ample go 2        # or: ample go verse-redo

Each entry shows the line name, distance from here (back to the split, then forward), the last message, markers (the real deal, releases, archived, automatic) and a play/listen hint. --all includes archived and automatic ones; --tree draws the graph. The UI graph is the same view: leaves are the highlighted ends, double-click one to go there.

Dropping a leaf: archive first, clean up later

Experiments that went nowhere are common, so dropping a dead-end leaf must be easy, but deleting stays dangerous. Two steps:

  1. ample drop <leaf> = mark as archived (the usual, safe action). Nothing is deleted: the leaf (and the revisions only it contains) fade out of leaves and log, stay in log --all and the graph's archive filter, and ample unarchive <leaf> or undo brings them back. Revisions shared with another line are never affected; only the part reachable from no other line counts as the leaf's own.
  2. ample cleanup = the real removal, later, on purpose. It targets archived leaves (never live ones) and is a purge: dry run with impact (revisions, space, baked blocks, releases that lose data), a backup suggestion, acceptance by typing the scope, a tombstone in the log. It can also be limited by age (--archived-older-than 30d) and shows which archived leaves it would take so single ones can be skipped.

Rules: the real deal and the revision you are on cannot be dropped; a leaf holding a sealed release is not dropped without a stronger confirmation; drop on a leaf with children offers to drop the whole branch (listing the children) or just that tip. Dropping a line with a name asks for that name.

$ ample drop 2            # verse-redo: marked archived (4 revisions), undo available
$ ample cleanup           # later: lists archived leaves, shows impact, suggests a backup, asks you to type the scope

The name of the real deal, and tags

Name of the main line. It is called studio and a new project starts with studio > garage (see "Studio and garage" below). The names are defaults and are not meant to change; they can be renamed if someone really wants to. Importing from git maps main/master to studio.

Tags are locked names for a revision. Meant for releases ("v1.0", "radio-edit"), but any revision can be tagged.

  • ample tag v1.0 [<rev>] creates a tag (default: here). A tag never moves by accident: tagging an existing name fails.
  • ample tag v1.0 <rev> --force --reason "..." re-tags. It is allowed but dangerous-lite: the old target stays in the tag's own history (ample tag --history v1.0) and in the operation log, so a re-tag can be undone and nothing is lost silently.
  • Removing a tag needs --force too and is logged; tag history is kept.
  • ample release can tag automatically (release v2 creates tag v2 on the sealed revision). A sealed release's tag cannot be force-moved to a different revision; a different revision means a new release and a new tag.
  • A tagged revision is protected: drop warns and cleanup skips it unless the tag is removed first on purpose.
  • Tags show in leaves, log and the graph as labels; go v1.0 works like any other target. Git mirror: tags map to git tags (annotated, with the hash of the release).

Checkpoints: a quick lookup table of named moments

A checkpoint is a light, named pointer to a revision, a quick way to find a moment again ("before the remix", "chorus works"). It replaces the earlier mark bookmark.

  • ample checkpoint ["name"] (UI: a button next to save). Without a name the default is a timestamp, e.g. cp-2026-10-02-1415. It records the revision you are on, and makes one first if there is unsaved work.
  • Unlike tags, checkpoints are not locked: they can be renamed, moved and removed freely (removing one deletes only the label, never the revision). That is what makes them cheap.
  • Tags stay for what must not move (releases, see above). A checkpoint can be promoted to a tag: ample tag v1.0 --from-checkpoint "chorus works".
  • ample checkpoints lists them (name, time, line, message), newest first, searchable; ample go "chorus works" jumps to one, and the graph shows them as small labels with a filter. They count as markers in leaves.
  • Automatic ones (auto/..., made before moves, promote, updates, migrations) are checkpoints too, but kept apart: hidden by default, grouped, and thinned out after a while (never the ones a revision or tag points at).
  • A checkpoint protects nothing from cleanup by itself (it is only a label); a dropped leaf's checkpoints show as archived with it. Tags do protect.

Protecting tags from tampering

Principle: moving a tag must be harder than making a revision, and never silent. Layers (1 to 4 default, 5 and 6 opt-in):

  1. No silent overwrite: an existing tag name cannot be reused by plain tag.
  2. Typing to re-tag: --force alone is not enough; the user types the tag name and a mandatory reason after seeing an impact summary (old and new target, whether a release or sealed hash hangs on it, who set it before). Same pattern as purge. Scripts need --accept "<tag>" --reason "..."; the UI has no shortcut.
  3. Tag types: release tags are created by release and can never move (a different revision means a new release and a new tag); normal tags can be re-tagged under layer 2; a tag can be frozen (ample tag --lock) so only unlock (same confirmation) releases it.
  4. Tag history: every create, move and delete is in the operation log (who, when, why) and reversible with undo. Backups and the git mirror carry the tag history.
  5. Signed tags (module signing, opt-in): a tag signed with the author's key; verify reports a move made without that key ("not set by the owner"), which also catches edits made outside AMPLE.
  6. Tags inside the sealed release: a release records its tag names and target hashes; verify flags a tag that no longer points at the sealed revision, also in a copy of the project elsewhere.

Studio and garage

  • A new project has two lines: studio (the top line, the real version) and below it garage, where you work; saves land on garage.
  • Promote: garage promoted to studio sets studio to that revision. The old studio tip stays in history.
  • Fork from studio: after a promote you can fork studio again, giving a new garage, and promote that one later too.
  • No merge: when the second garage is promoted, the first garage is no longer reachable in the daily view (only through commit history), the same rule as archived leaves.
  • Going back to a commit rebuilds the tree as it was. Every promote and fork records where each line stood (a snapshot of the pointers, kept with the operation log). ample go <rev> then asks: "Should studio be replaced too?"
    • No (default): only garage (and any other children of studio) is restored, as a child of the current studio. studio is not overwritten.
    • Yes: studio also returns to its state back then; the old top is kept as an archive and undo reverses it.
  • Releases are tags (locked, see above) on any line, recommended from studio. There is no separate top level for releases.

Temporary read-only checkout (look, rebuild, leave)

Any revision, tag or release can be opened temporarily and read-only, for example to rebuild an older release. This is ample go <rev|tag> --peek (UI: "Open read-only"); it is a mode, not a move of here.

  • Nothing in history can change: saves, checkpoints and promotes are refused while peeking. The banner says what you are on ("read-only: v1.0 (tag), 2026-09-12").
  • Rebuild is allowed: render/master and verify --repro run on the checked-out sources, lock and baked data. Results go to a scratch area (.ample/scratch/<rev>/), never into the project's takes or releases, so the sealed release stays untouched. Compare the rebuilt hash with the sealed one: same hash = reproduced; different = reported with the toolprint differences (a tool or model from back then may be missing: verify --present says what).
  • Leaving is free: ample go --back (or closing the peek) returns to where you were, with your unsaved work exactly as it was. The scratch area is removed on leave, or kept on request (--keep-scratch) and listed for cleanup.
  • Turning it into work: "work from here" (ample go <rev> without --peek) forks as described above. A rebuild you want to keep can be saved as a new take or release only from a normal (non-peek) state.

Clean-up keeps a safety copy of dropped lines (2026-10-20)

Dropping a line is reversible, and so is the clean-up that follows it: before the clean-up removes the content of a dropped line it copies it to .ample/history-archive/<timestamp>/ (manifest.json with line name, revision ids and files, plus blobs/<hash> with the exact bytes). The folder is built as <timestamp>.partial, every blob is read back and hashed, and only then is it renamed. If writing or verifying fails the clean-up removes nothing and stops with AMP5247. The dry run lists the dropped lines that will be archived and the size of the archive. Bring back puts the content of a dropped line back from the archive when the live copy is gone (without an archive it still fails cleanly with AMP5246). Nothing in AMPLE deletes the archive; the storage clean-up does not scan or remove the folder, but it counts the archived revisions as references so the takes they name stay protected.

History management (detail)

Status (2026-10-02): design sketch from a brainstorm. Nothing here is built or tested. History v1 holds the decisions (lines, studio and garage, promote, tags, checkpoints, drop and cleanup); this page works them out into a data model, operations, screens and scenarios. The clickable sketch in sketch/ shows the screens.

1. Principles

  1. Nothing is lost silently. Every move is a pointer move recorded in the operation log; only cleanup and purge remove data, and both are dangerous acts with a dry run, a backup suggestion and typed acceptance.
  2. Everything stays reachable until it is deliberately removed: any revision, any line (also archived ones), any earlier arrangement of the lines.
  3. Revisions are immutable and tamper-evident (their id is a hash of content and parent).
  4. No merges in v1. Lines diverge; one is promoted. "Adopt this block" and structure-aware merge are tracked in Future ideas.
  5. Natural navigation is by line, leaf, checkpoint and tag; hashes are the exception.
  6. Two audiences, one model: a simple view that shows what matters, an advanced view that shows everything.

2. Data model (SQLite in .ample/history.db)

revision   id (hash of content+parent), parent, line_at_creation, author, time, message,
           kind (save | auto | adopt | migration), content_ref, summary_json
content    id (hash), sources_tree_hash, lock_hash, settings_hash, cuts_json, baked_refs_json, modules_json
line       name, tip, forked_from (revision), role (studio | garage | fork), state (live | archived), created, renamed_from
tag        name, target, type (normal | release | frozen), created_by, created_at          + tag_history(name, target, op, by, at, reason)
checkpoint name, target, auto (0|1), created_at
arrangement id, taken_at, studio_tip, lines_json   one row per promote and fork: where every line stood (so "restore the tree as it was" works)
operation  id, time, by, kind, args_json, before_json, after_json, danger (0..3), reason     the operation log (undo and redo walk this)
tombstone  op_id, scope, what_was_removed_json, size, backup_ref                              what cleanup/purge removed
release    id, tag, revision, sealed_hash, kind (recipe-exact | data-exact), lineage_json
  • A revision id is hash(parent id + content id + author + time + message), so history cannot be rewritten without changing ids; with the signing module the id is also signed.
  • Content is separate from the revision so identical states share rows; sources are stored as a tree of file hashes (a snapshot), not as diffs.
  • Takes and baked data are not in the database; revisions reference them by hash (take bank, see Bake).
  • Secrets are never in history; a revision records only which credential name and version it needed (see section 9).

3. What a revision contains

| In the revision | Not in the revision | | --- | --- | | Sources (.amplet, lyrics, MIDI, chords, packs list), ample.lock, cuts, which baked blocks are used, the enabled modules, project settings that affect results, the layout of the block graph | Credentials, machine-local settings, the cache and scratch, the take bank files themselves (referenced by hash), unsaved drafts | Layout-only changes (moving a block on the canvas) are saved but marked layout in the summary, so they do not look like musical changes in the history and can be hidden by a filter.

4. Operations (what each does, how risky)

| Operation | Effect on pointers | Undo | Danger | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | save | new revision on the line you are on (forks by itself if you are not on a tip) | undo | 0 | | checkpoint | adds a light label (renamable, movable, removable) | undo | 0 | | tag | adds a locked label | undo | 0 | | go | moves here; if the target studio differs from now, asks "replace studio too?" (default no) | undo | 0 | | go --peek | read-only checkout; rebuilds go to scratch/ | leave | 0 | | fork | new line from a revision | undo | 0 | | promote | moves studio; old tip kept as archive/studio-N; no merge | undo | 1 | | drop | marks a leaf archived | unarchive / undo | 1 | | rename line | renames, keeps renamed_from | undo | 1 | | re-tag / unlock tag | moves a locked tag; old target in tag_history | undo | 2 (typed name and reason) | | cleanup | removes archived leaves and unreferenced data for real | no (only from a backup) | 2 (dry run, backup suggestion, typed scope, tombstone) | | purge | removes chosen revisions or credential versions for real | no | 3 (like cleanup, stronger for anything holding a sealed release) | | undo / redo | steps through the operation log (does not undo cleanup/purge) | redo | 0 | Unsaved work is never a revision. When you move away from unsaved changes, AMPLE takes an automatic checkpoint (a draft revision of kind auto, hidden by default) first, so nothing is lost; a crash leaves a draft that is offered back on the next open.

5. The History screen (anatomy)

┌ toolbar: [Save] [Checkpoint] [Promote] [Fork]  search [___________]  filters ▾   view: (•) Simple ( ) Advanced   [Compare] [Export] [Cleanup]
├ graph (lanes: studio, garage, forks)         ┬ detail of the selected revision
│  ★ = studio   ◯ = here   ⚑ checkpoint   🏷 tag  │  message, author, time, line, tags, checkpoints
│  faded = archived                             │  changed blocks, layout-only flag, takes used
│                                               │  buttons: Go · Look only · Make studio · Fork · Checkpoint · Tag · Compare
├ leaves list (ample leaves)                    ┴
└ status line: here r12 (garage, tip) · studio r9 · 3 unsaved changes · last backup 2 days ago
  • Simple view: the recent revisions plus everything that matters (tips, studio, here, tags, user checkpoints), compressed with "... 14 older" markers. Archived lines and automatic checkpoints are hidden.
  • Advanced view: every revision, archived lines (faded), automatic checkpoints, ids and parent links, tools and baked counts.
  • Filters: text (message, block name), author, line, "touched block ...", tag or checkpoint only, date range, kind (save, auto), layout-only on/off.
  • Keyboard: arrows move along a line and between lines at forks, Enter = go, Space = look only, P = promote, F = fork, C = checkpoint, T = tag, / = search.
  • Everywhere else: the header always shows the line you are on and the studio revision; the Structure browser (left) is the same data as a tree.

The branch tree and the "branch laid out" view

  • Structure panel (left), simple view: only the path from the root to the branch you are on plus its direct leaves (branches forked from it), and a + New leaf under button that forks from where you are. Recent revisions of the active branch sit in a collapsed list. This replaces long revision lists in the tree.
  • Structure panel, advanced view: the whole branch tree (parent to children), archived branches faded.
  • Clicking a branch name opens the Branches tab: one row laid out left to right: the root (studio) on the left, an arrow to each branch on the path, the focused branch highlighted as THIS BRANCH, and its direct leaves stacked on the right. The row scrolls sideways and starts centred on the focused branch. Each branch is a box with its tip message, where it forked from, a strip of revision dots (the dot where the next branch forks is outlined, the dot you are on is ringed) and buttons Go, Look, + Leaf, Drop or Unarchive. Clicking another box refocuses the row.
  • Branch manager (dedicated view): a switch above the canvas replaces the block view with the whole hierarchy as a scrollable tree (root left, siblings stacked, any number of leaves per branch and leaves of leaves). Focusing a branch there also centres it in the Branches tab; you can fold subtrees, search, show archived, rename, go, look, add a leaf and drop. The Branches tab under the canvas deliberately shows only the direct line.
  • Parent of a branch is derived, not stored: the line of the revision its first revision was forked from. Promote only moves studio; it does not change who is whose parent.

6. Compare

Pick two revisions (or a revision and "now"). The result is structural, not a text diff:

  • Blocks: added, removed, renamed (detected by stable block id), moved (layout only), changed.
  • Parameters: old to new per block, with the node seed unchanged or changed.
  • Links: added and removed connections.
  • Takes: same take hash, different take hash, or baked versus recipe. A changed dynamic block offers Listen A/B (plays the two takes, aligned).
  • Text: the .amplet diff as a secondary tab.
  • Verdict line: "audio probably changed in: chorus_vox, mixer, master" (derived from which blocks and their downstream changed), "nothing audible changed: layout only".

7. Search

An index over messages, authors, touched block ids and parameter names (kept in SQLite). Queries like "where did chorus_vox's seed change", "all revisions by alex in October", "everything tagged release". Results open in the graph with the matches highlighted.

8. Going back, forking and restoring the tree (worked scenarios)

  1. Go back 5, save, then 1 back and 5 up. go ~5 moves here. save from a non-tip forks a new line automatically (named from the fork point). go ~1 then go +5 follow the path you walked (like a browser's back and forward); at a fork the arrow keys choose a line.
  2. Promote. garage tip r12 becomes studio. The old studio tip r9 is kept as archive/studio-r9. A second garage forked from the new studio and promoted later makes the first garage unreachable in the daily view (still in the graph through "show archived" and in advanced).
  3. Restore the tree as it was. go r7 asks: "Should studio be replaced too?" No (default): only garage (and other children of studio) come back, as children of the current studio. Yes: studio also moves back to what it was at r7, the old studio goes to the archive, undo reverses it. This uses the arrangement rows.
  4. Experiment that went nowhere. drop the leaf (archived, undoable). Weeks later cleanup lists archived leaves with their size and impact; you choose which to remove for real, after the backup suggestion.
  5. Rebuild an old release. go v1.0 --peek opens it read-only; Build runs into scratch/; compare the rebuilt hash with the sealed release; leave and everything is as before.

9. Credentials have their own timeline

Credentials are not part of revisions. The vault has its own numbered timeline (added, rotated, revoked, by whom) with sealed values. A revision records which credential and version it needed; verify reports "needs weather_api v2, current is v3". Going back in the project never restores or exposes an old secret. Old credential versions can be purged on their own (dangerous act). See Backup for how the vault travels.

10. Releases in the history

A release is a locked tag plus a sealed release record (hash, recipe-exact or data-exact, lineage based on / remix of). It can sit on any line, recommended on studio. The history screen marks releases, and the lineage view shows how releases derive from each other (also across projects, by uuid). A sealed release's tag cannot be force-moved; a new revision means a new release and a new tag. Tag protection layers are in History v1.

11. Storage and size

  • Revisions are small (hashes and JSON); the size is the take bank and baked data.
  • ample size reports by line and by revision: how much each line uniquely holds, so cleanup choices are informed ("verse-redo holds 1.2 GB that nothing else uses").
  • Cleanup candidates: archived leaves, takes referenced by no revision, tag or checkpoint, old auto checkpoints beyond a policy (manual for now), scratch and cache.
  • Never a candidate without extra confirmation: anything a sealed release, a tag or a user checkpoint refers to.

12. Integrity

  • Single writer per project (instance lock); SQLite WAL; every operation is one transaction.
  • ample verify-history recomputes revision ids and checks parents; ample doctor includes it (quick: recent revisions; full: all).
  • With signing, tags and releases are signed; a move made outside AMPLE (editing the database) shows up as "not set by the owner".
  • A rolling daily copy of history.db protects against corruption.

13. Export and mirror

  • Export a slice (ample export --scope line:garage or tag:v1.0 or checkpoint:"chorus works") as a .ample file with chosen contents; opening it creates a new project or, later, imports the line into an existing one (see Future ideas: pull and push).
  • Git mirror (module): one-way mirror of lines and tags with the release hash in annotated tags; conversions both ways keep raw git objects for a lossless round trip.

14. CLI twins

ample log [--all] [--tree]        ample leaves [--all]        ample go <line|leaf|~N|+N|checkpoint|tag|hash> [--peek] [--with-studio]
ample save -m "..."               ample checkpoint ["name"]   ample checkpoints      ample tag <name> [<rev>]   ample tag --history <name>
ample fork [<name>]               ample promote [<rev>]       ample drop <leaf>       ample unarchive <leaf>     ample cleanup
ample compare <a> <b>             ample undo / redo           ample ops               ample size              ample verify-history
ample export --scope <line|tag|checkpoint> --contents sources,baked,takes,history

15. Open questions

  1. Should a timeline scrubber (drag through revisions with a quick audio preview of the master) be part of v1 or a later nicety?
  2. How long are auto drafts kept, and when are they thinned (manual for now; propose a gentle default later)?
  3. Do layout-only changes get their own revisions, or are they folded into the next real change?
  4. Should compare show sound differences measured on the rendered takes (loudness, spectral change) next to the structural ones?
  5. Is the operation log shown to the user as a full panel, or only through undo and redo and the Log tab?

Project management

Status (2026-10-11): partial. The CLI supports ample new, ample open, ample doctor [--env], ample instances and project inspection; ample open attaches to or starts the server for a project. The lifecycle, template and management sections below include planned behavior and are not a claim that every listed UI, CLI or API operation is implemented.

Project management and history management (History management) are the two things the whole tool leans on, so this page goes into detail. It covers what a project is, where its data lives, how it is created, opened, copied, archived, moved and deleted, how settings are scoped, how health is checked and how format changes are migrated.

1. Vocabulary

Term Meaning
Project A folder that contains a mandatory .ample/ folder. Everything the project needs to reproduce its songs is inside it or reachable through its links.
Home The per-user AMPLE folder (for example %APPDATA%\ample or ~/.config/ample): global links, recent projects, plugin and model catalog, user templates, global settings. Never part of a project or a backup of a project.
Engine The running ample serve process. One engine can serve several projects at once (each in its own browser tab).
Link A named folder outside the project that is exposed in the folder browser (see Tech, "Linked folders"). Global or per project, read-only or read-write.
Take bank The immutable, hash-addressed store of rendered audio and baked data of a project.

2. What is in a project folder

my-song/                         the project (any name; it can be renamed or moved)
  song.amplet  lyrics/  midi/  chords/  packs/ ...     user content (sources)
  ample.lock                     pinned tools, packs, external data
  .ample/                        mandatory; AMPLE's own data
    project.json                 id (uuid), name, format version, created, master seed, modules, main line names
    history.db                   SQLite: revisions, lines, tags, checkpoints, operation log, tombstones
    takes/                       the take bank (hash-addressed, immutable)
    data/                        baked data blocks (hash-addressed)
    links.json                   project links (uuid, name, read-only flag, relative path hint); global links live in Home with their uuid
    assets.json                  uuids of project assets (assigned the first time AMPLE sees them; survive rename and move)
    vault/                       sealed credential store and its own timeline (no plain secrets)
    plugins.lock                 pinned plugin versions and toolprints
    cache/                       build cache (disposable, safe to delete)
    scratch/                     read-only checkouts and rebuilds (disposable)
    lock                         instance lock (pid, host, heartbeat)
    logs/                        engine logs (no prompts or lyrics: see privacy below)
  .ampleignore                   what the source scan and snapshots skip

Rules:

  • Disposable means safe to delete at any time without losing information: cache/, scratch/, logs/.
  • Precious means loss is permanent: history.db, takes/, data/, vault/, the sources and ample.lock. Backups cover these (profiles decide how much, see Backup).
  • project.json holds a uuid, not the path, so a project can be moved, renamed or opened from a backup restore and still be recognised in Recent and in the lineage records of releases.
  • A folder with sources but without .ample/ is not a project; the app offers "Make this an AMPLE project" (creates .ample/, first revision "adopted folder", scans the sources).

3. Lifecycle

Create

A wizard (UI) or ample new <folder>:

  1. Name and location. The folder name defaults to a slug of the name; the name itself is free text.
  2. Template (see section 4).
  3. Modules to enable (all off except core by default, see Modules).
  4. Master seed: random (default) or typed. It is shown once and stored in project.json; changing it later is a deliberate, logged act, because it changes every derived seed (and therefore every dynamic result not baked).
  5. Links: pick global links to use here, add project links.
  6. First revision: the project starts with the lines studio and garage, one revision "new project" on studio, you are on garage (see History v1).
  7. The engine writes .ample/, takes the instance lock and opens the project.

Open

  • Recent list in the Projects manager (name, path, last opened, line and revision you were on, health badge, size).
  • Open folder: a folder picker served by the engine (it only shows what the engine may see: the user's chosen roots and links). A folder with .ample/ opens; a folder without offers adoption.
  • Drag and drop a folder or a .ample export file onto the Projects manager; a .ample file is never opened in place: it is restored or imported into a new folder first (see section 7).
  • URL: http://127.0.0.1:5174/?project=<uuid> opens a known project (tabs can be bookmarked).
  • On open the engine takes the instance lock, checks the format version, runs a quick health check (a few seconds, never a full scrub) and restores your last view (line, revision, open tab). If you left unsaved work it is offered back (see History management, "Unsaved work").

Switch and close

Each browser tab is bound to one project. Closing the tab releases nothing by itself; the engine releases the instance lock when the last tab of a project closes (with a short grace period) or on shutdown. Unsaved work is kept as a draft, not lost.

Rename, move, duplicate

  • Rename: changes the name in project.json (and optionally the folder name). The uuid stays.
  • Move: moving the folder is fine while it is closed; the Recent entry then says "moved? locate" and relinks by uuid when you point at it.
  • Duplicate offers three explicit choices: fork with history (new uuid, history and takes copied or hard-linked, the lineage records "copy of"), fresh start from the current state (new uuid, no history, takes referenced by baked data only), template from this (strips takes and history, keeps structure).

Archive and delete

  • Archive marks a project as archived in Home (hidden from the default list, nothing changes on disk). It can offer to compress takes/ and cache/ later.
  • Delete project is a dangerous act (see section 9): it shows what would be lost (revisions, takes in MB, releases that exist nowhere else), offers a backup first and asks for the project name to be typed. The default action is move to the system trash, not a hard delete.

4. Project templates

New-project templates are folders with an .ample/template.json and starter content: | Template | Gives you | | --- | --- | | Empty | Core only, one tempo, no tracks. | | Instrumental | Drums, bass, chords and a mixer block wired to a master chain. | | Song with AI voice | The above plus lyrics, an AI voice block (plugin required) and a variants set. | | Remix | Import audio or MIDI blocks, an overlap track, based on and remix of ready. | Templates live in Home (yours), in a project (shared with its collaborators later) or in a pack. A template can pin plugin versions and links. "Save as template" strips history, takes, vault and secrets.

5. Settings and their scopes

| Scope | Where | Shared in exports/backups | Examples | | --- | --- | --- | --- | | Global (user) | Home | no | author name, default view (simple or advanced), global links, plugin catalog, default templates, theme, engine port | | Project | .ample/project.json | yes | name, modules, assist level, tempo default, output folder, project links (without machine paths, see below), storage policy, backup profile and reminder interval, history view default | | Machine-local | .ample/local.json (git-ignored, never exported) | no | absolute paths of links on this machine, plugin install paths, GPU/CPU choices | Precedence: machine-local > project > global > built-in default. A project link records a logical name and, where portable, a project-relative path; the machine-local file maps names to real paths on this computer, so a restored project asks once "where is Samples on this machine?" instead of breaking.

Project settings that matter most:

  • Modules: quality, credits, signing, git-mirror, secrets, lyrics (opt-in; turning one on is a normal revision).
  • Assist: off, diff, button or auto.
  • Output folder: a read-write link or the project folder; a read-only link can never be chosen as output.
  • Storage policy: where big audio lives (inside, LFS, AMPLE store, external with accept-until), and the warnings that go with it.
  • Backups: profile (minimal, standard, complete), reminder after N days or N revisions, last backup time shown in the Projects manager.
  • History: default view (simple or advanced), cleanup is on request only (for now), automatic checkpoints are manual (for now).

6. Identity

Every revision records an author (from the global setting, default the OS user). It is a label for credits and history, not authentication: a local tool has no accounts. With the signing module the author also has a key (the private key is not in backups by default).

7. Import, export, backup and restore

  • Backup (ample backup) writes one .ample file: a zip with manifest.json (project uuid, name, format version, profile, what is inside and what is deliberately left out, tool and plugin versions), the history, takes and data per profile, and optionally the sealed vault. See Backup.
  • Partial export (ample export) takes a scope (project, line, tag, release or checkpoint) and a choice of contents (sources only, plus baked data, plus takes and audio, plus history, plus credentials sealed and off by default). It says plainly what is missing so the result can still be opened.
  • Restore always goes into a new folder and never overwrites. It verifies hashes, reports what is missing (and why), asks once for the machine-local things (link locations, plugin availability) and then opens like any project. A restored project keeps its uuid unless a project with that uuid is already known, in which case you choose "restore as copy" (new uuid, lineage "restored from").
  • Import handles: an .ample file (restore as above), a git repository (via the git mirror in reverse), an old recipe or .ggufmusic, audio and MIDI into blocks.
  • Round trip guarantee (goal): backup, then restore on another machine, then verify --hash passes; verify --repro passes for everything recipe-exact on a declared platform class.

8. Health and maintenance

ample doctor (UI: Health panel with traffic lights and a "fix" button per item): | Check | Depth | Fix offered | | --- | --- | --- | | Instance lock is ours / stale lock | quick | take over (typed, shows pid, host and last heartbeat) | | history.db integrity (PRAGMA integrity_check) and hash chain | quick / full | restore the last good copy (a rolling history.db.bak per day) | | Format version vs this AMPLE | quick | migrate (with automatic backup and checkpoint) or open read-only | | Links present and reachable; read-only flag respected | quick | relocate, remove | | Tools and plugins present with the pinned toolprints | quick | install, or accept the difference (reported in verify) | | Take bank scrub (recompute hashes) | full (slow, on request) | re-fetch from backup, mark take as lost | | Unreferenced takes and baked data (size) | quick | cleanup (dangerous act, see history management) | | cache/ and scratch/ size | quick | clear | | Free disk space vs take bank growth | quick | warn | | Cloud-synced or network folder detected | quick | warn (SQLite and sync tools do not mix) | | Last backup age | quick | back up now | ample doctor --fix only does safe fixes (clear cache and scratch, rotate logs); anything that removes precious data goes through the dangerous-act pattern.

9. The dangerous-act pattern (shared by project and history)

Delete project, purge, cleanup, re-tag, unlock a frozen tag, change the master seed, take over a stale lock, restore over a known uuid. All of them:

  1. Show a dry run: exactly what changes, how much space, which releases or lineage links lose data, what stays untouched.
  2. Suggest a backup and offer to make it right there.
  3. Ask for typed acceptance (the project name, the tag name or the scope), never a bare yes; in scripts --accept "<what>" --reason "...".
  4. Leave a tombstone in the operation log (who, when, what, why). The UI uses one red dialog for all of them so the shape is always recognisable.

10. Concurrency, safety and privacy

  • One writer per project. The instance lock (pid, host, heartbeat) stops two engines writing to the same .ample/. A second engine can open the project read-only (peek mode for the whole project) or take over a stale lock after the typed confirmation.
  • Crash safety: SQLite in WAL mode; the take bank only ever adds files (write to temp, fsync, rename); a rolling daily copy of history.db.
  • Path safety: the engine serves only paths inside the project and its links; .. never escapes; read-only links are never written to, also not by plugins.
  • Privacy: logs and the health report never contain lyrics, prompts or file names of takes; secrets live only in the sealed vault and never in project.json, exports (unless sealed on purpose) or logs.
  • Network: the server binds to 127.0.0.1; remote use is explicit, with a token and an SSH tunnel (see Tech).

11. Format versions and migration

project.json carries format (an integer). On open:

  • Same format: open.
  • Older format: the app offers to migrate. A migration takes an automatic backup and checkpoint first, runs in a transaction and is recorded in the operation log. A failed migration leaves the project as it was.
  • Newer format: open read-only with a clear message (never try to write); unknown fields are always preserved on write by this version.

12. CLI twins of the UI

ample new <folder> [--template instrumental]     ample open <folder>        ample projects [--archived]
ample rename "<name>"      ample duplicate --with-history|--fresh|--as-template      ample archive|unarchive
ample delete-project       (dry run, backup suggestion, typed acceptance)
ample backup [--profile standard]      ample restore <file.ample> <new-folder>      ample export --scope tag:v1.0 ...
ample import <file|git-url|recipe>     ample doctor [--full] [--fix]      ample links [add|remove|list|set-readonly]

13. Open questions

  1. Should Recent and project tags/colours live only in Home, or should a project be able to carry a colour for its tab?
  2. Duplicate with history: copy the take bank or hard-link it (fast, but ties the two projects to the same files)?
  3. Is a project allowed to be opened from inside a cloud-synced folder at all (warn, or refuse)?
  4. How is the master seed change handled: a new project (fork) instead of an in-place change?
  5. Do project templates travel in the .ample export when asked ("export as template")?

Project layout and safety (as built)

Status (2026-10-02): implemented in chunk 40 (Windows verified; Linux runs when CI first runs).

A project is a folder with a mandatory .ample/ folder. Everything the user writes (songs, lyrics, chords) lives next to it; everything AMPLE manages lives inside .ample/. The design background is in Project management; this page describes what the code does.

<project>/
  *.amplet, lyrics/, chords/ ...     the user's sources
  .ample/
    project.json                     id, name, created, format version, master seed, settings
    history.db                       history database (chunk 50)
    takes/  data/                    the takebank (chunk 42)
    blackbox/                        AMPLE Redux journal (legacy storage path; chunk 45)
    locks/instance.lock              held by the one writer (operating-system lock)
    locks/instance.json              heartbeat: process, machine, started, last seen
    tmp/                             scratch, safe to delete while the project is closed
    backups/                         copies of project.json made before a format upgrade

project.json

Canonical JSON (fixed property order, indented, LF). The master seed is stored as a decimal string. A new project's master seed is derived from its id unless given. The id never changes when the folder is moved or renamed. Settings: AMPLE Redux (budget 10 GiB, 90 days full detail, a year thinned), cleanup (no automatic age limit), mounts (filled by the library, chunk 85), default engine.

Format versions and upgrades

The current format is 1. Opening a project for writing upgrades an older format: the old project.json is first copied to .ample/backups/project.v<N>.<time>.json, then the upgrade steps run and the result replaces the file atomically. Opening read-only never upgrades (AMP5209). A project made by a newer AMPLE is refused (AMP5206). Fault tests prove that an error at any step leaves either the old or the new file complete, and the backup intact.

One writer

The writer holds an operating-system lock on .ample/locks/instance.lock and writes the heartbeat. A second writer is refused with AMP5204 that names the holder; read-only opening always works. A held lock is never broken automatically; taking over is a dangerous act that comes with the history work (chunks 50 and 77). ample doctor reports whether the lock is held or only an old heartbeat remains.

Atomic writes

Project files are written to a temporary file (*.ample-tmp) in the same folder, flushed to disk, renamed over the target, and the folder is flushed where the platform allows it. A crash leaves the old file, the new file, or a harmless leftover that the doctor reports (AMP5213).

Safe paths

All project paths go through ProjectPath: relative only, no .. escape (AMP5201), no invalid characters, trailing dot or space or Windows reserved name (AMP5202), and no symbolic link or junction that leads outside the project or a registered link (AMP5203).

Control: seeds, freeze, variants, regeneration (as built, chunk 58)

Seeds are stored per block and locked by default (derived from the master seed); changing one needs an unlock first (AMP5260: it probably makes reproduction impossible), and every change is kept in the seed history. The freeze ladder is read from the block header: nothing (free), freeze seeds, freeze plan (the melody output of the selected take is passed back to the renderer as a pinned input and becomes part of the plan), or bake with a selected take (that exact take is used and nothing is rendered; if its data is missing the build says so with AMP5221 and does not render). Variants: ample variants makes several takes of one block, each with its own seed derived from the master seed; asking again gives the same ones; you choose one, keep others and discard the rest (a tombstone). Safe regeneration (ample regen, see Regeneration safety): the selected take is never touched; the new result is verified against it; identical means "same result"; different becomes an open decision, stored in the database, whose default is to restore (keep) the previous take, so a crash or a closed dialog leaves the old take in place. Replacing the take is a dangerous act. ample verify-reproduction re-renders the take's own plan only to check, and the result goes into the take's reproduction history. ample explain says what each kind of edit does at the block's freeze level.

Build (as built, chunk 55)

ample build <song> orders the blocks by their connections and, for each block, builds a plan from its source (type, name, class, parts, parameters and connections; not the bake, lock or refresh flags), the takes of its inputs, its derived seeds, the renderer and the settings. If a take for that plan exists it is used (a cache hit); otherwise the plan is stored first (the Always rule), the block is rendered and the take committed. Changing one block therefore re-renders it and what depends on it, and nothing else. --preview 5:4 renders four bars from bar 5 at a low sample rate (a separate plan from the full build); ample bake <song> <block> renders at full quality and adds bake to the block header; ample play writes a preview WAV. The built-in renderers (midi-clip, drums, bass, piano, mixer, master, group) use integer-only synthesis (fixed-point oscillators, tables computed with decimal arithmetic), so the same song gives the same bytes on every machine. Blocks without a renderer (AI voices and other plugin blocks) are skipped with AMP5251 until plugins exist.

History (as built, chunk 50)

ample history|checkpoint|tag|fork|go|peek|promote|drop|cleanup. The snapshot of a state is the set of source files (.amplet, .amplelrc, .lrc, .chordpro, .lyr, .chords), each stored once in the takebank; a node is immutable and stored in history.db. A new project has the lines studio (the real version) and garage (work happens here). Checkpoint snapshots only when something changed. Go first checkpoints unsaved work automatically (kind auto), so switching never loses anything, then restores the target's files through the command bus. Peek reads another state without changing anything. Promote shows the changes first (--yes does it) and replaces studio's head with garage's; the old state stays in the history. Tags are locked; moving or removing one, dropping a line (archive, recoverable) and cleanup are dangerous acts with dry run, typed acceptance, reason and tombstones. Cleanup only removes file contents that no active line and no tag can reach, and never content used by a take.

Command path and AMPLE Redux (as built, chunk 45)

Every state change is an ICommand run by the CommandBus: the pre-image (what is about to be overwritten) is captured, a start record is written to the journal and made durable, the change is applied, then an ok or failed record follows. If the journal cannot be written the command is not run (AMP5230). AMPLE Redux currently uses the compatible .ample/blackbox/ storage path and *.seg files (JSON lines, each with a CRC32C and the SHA-256 of the previous record, so a changed record is detected). A torn last line (a crash while writing) is dropped on open; a damaged record in the middle is never repaired away: the file stays as evidence and new records go to a new segment. A command with a start but no outcome record is interrupted (ample recover); the legacy ample blackbox restore <seq> command restores a file from a pre-image as a new command. A copy of the journal tail is kept in the user's home (%LOCALAPPDATA%/Ample/blackbox-mirror/<project id>/). Retention: full detail for 90 days, then hourly summaries for a year, within a 10 GiB budget (the legacy ample blackbox compact command; the newest segment is never thinned). The journal is not encrypted (optional encryption is chunk 92). Dangerous acts share one contract: dry run, backup suggestion, typed acceptance, reason, tombstone record (AMP5232).

Commands

ample new <folder> [--name N] [--seed N] creates a project. ample open <folder> attaches to or starts its local server; ample project open <folder> opens it for writing, prints a summary and releases the lock. ample project info <folder> prints the summary read-only. ample doctor <folder> checks structure, project file, lock state, leftovers, unknown entries and free disk space against the AMPLE Redux budget, and changes nothing.

Library (chunk 85)

The catalog is per user (library.db in the home folder), not per project. A project keeps ample.lock in its root (assets, packs and plugins pinned by hash), an assets/ folder for imported files (each with a .provenance.json), and the ids of its project links in project.json settings (mounts). A writable linked folder carries .ample-catalog.json. See the library manager.

Takebank and plans (as built)

Status (2026-10-02): implemented in chunk 42 (Windows verified; Linux runs when CI first runs).

The takebank stores everything AMPLE has ever rendered, immutably, together with the plan (the complete recipe) it was made from. It is what makes a song safe: the stored take is the guarantee, the seed is only a bonus (see Determinism and Regeneration safety).

The Always rule, enforced three times

  1. API: Takebank.BeginAsync(plan) stores the plan first (a file and a database row) and returns a ticket; ticket.CommitAsync(...) is the only way to create a take, and a ticket works once.
  2. Database: a take row needs a plan row. A trigger refuses a take without a stored plan even for someone who opens the database directly with foreign keys switched off (AMP5220). Plans, takes and their data references can never be updated or deleted (AMP5224); dropping a take is a tombstone flag, the record stays.
  3. Files: the plan is also written as .ample/takes/plans/<hash>.plan.json and the take as .ample/takes/<xx>/<hash>.take.json, a plain copy that survives a damaged database.

Plans

A plan holds: project id, block uuid and path, hash of the block's source, inputs (data or take ids with toolprints), seeds, the rngVersion, plugin id and version, toolprint, settings, intent (preview, bake, variant, freeze, verify) and the parent plan (for regenerations). Its canonical JSON is frozen (fixed property order, seeds sorted by name, other objects sorted by key, no white space, non-ASCII escaped, schema tag ample-plan/1) and the plan id is sha256: plus the hash of that text. The time is not part of it, so the same recipe has the same id. spec-tests/plans/canonical-golden.json pins the canonical text and ids; changing the form needs a new schema tag.

Data and takes

Data blobs are content-addressed (sha256:<hex>, stored as .ample/data/<xx>/<hex>), streamed and hashed while written to a temporary file, then moved into place, so identical content is stored once even when several writers race. A take is its plan plus its data (role and id per blob); its id is the hash of those, so committing the same outputs for the same plan gives the same take. Every render attempt is recorded (started, completed, failed, cancelled, with the reason): a failed or cancelled render keeps its plan, and an attempt that stays started was interrupted.

Reading, verifying, orphans, sizes

  • ReadTake returns the take with its plan; blobs that are not on disk are listed as missing instead of failing, so the take can be re-rendered from its plan or restored from a backup (AMP5221 when the data itself is opened).
  • VerifyAsync rehashes the data and reports missing files, wrong sizes and bit rot.
  • Blobs that no take references (an interrupted put) are found and quarantined, never deleted.
  • Sizes are available per take and per block (distinct data counted once).

AI proposal builds may open the active project's takebank through Takebank.OpenReadOnly. Exact-plan audio is copied into the disposable proposal takebank; no plan, attempt, take, data row or blob is written to the source project. Existing project files that predate the setting use this cache by default; the AI setting can disable it.

Commands

ample takes list|show|verify [--project P] and ample plan show <take>; a take id can be given as a unique prefix.

Storage: the takebank, protection and clean-up

Status (2026-10-11): overview, protection rules, clean-up (UI, CLI, API), soft limit, options, size and time estimate, compressed takes and the data path on another drive are built. Finals are also built; see Finals. Remaining storage plan parts: plan/storage.

Every render is kept as a take in .ample/data, so a song never renders twice. Over time that adds up (a dubstep session of a day reached 22 GB). The Storage page (Projects, Storage) and ample storage show where the space goes and give it back safely.

What is never removed

One function decides (StorageService.Classify); nothing else does. A take is protected when it is:

  • chosen (the selected take of a block), a variant or part of a regeneration decision;
  • baked or pinned: its id is named in a song or module of the project, or in any history revision (so tags, checkpoints and releases keep their takes);
  • the current take of a block (the newest), and the takes it was made from;
  • a final;
  • younger than the keep window (default one hour), so a running build or an open preview is never touched.

Everything else is reclaimable: superseded takes (an older take of a block that has a newer one, beyond the "older takes to keep" option) and takes whose data is already missing. A removed take is tombstoned (its record and plan stay) and its data is deleted (or moved to the archive folder); when the song needs it again it simply renders again.

Never touched: the renders/ folder and every other file of yours.

Dry run, impact, progress

  • Studio: Projects, Storage: a bar (protected / can be given back), the reasons, the free space of the drive; "See what a clean-up would do…" shows the impact (takes and GB per reason and per block, free space before and after, what stays protected); "Clean up" runs it in the background with a progress bar and Cancel (it stops between items and leaves a consistent store).
  • CLI: ample storage show, ample storage clean (dry run, prints a fingerprint), ample storage clean --accept <fingerprint>, ample storage settings --soft-limit-gb 10 --keep-superseded 1 --archive-path D:\ample-archive.
  • API: GET /api/storage, POST /api/storage/plan, POST /api/storage/clean (the fingerprint of the dry run must still match), GET /api/storage/status, POST /api/storage/cancel, POST /api/storage/settings; progress also goes to the event stream (storage.progress, storage.done).
  • Temporary working files (finished AI tasks, .ample/tmp) older than a day are part of the dry run.

Soft limit

softLimitGb (default 10; 0 is off) never deletes anything: when the project is over it, or the drive has less than 5 GB free, the studio shows a hint with the real numbers and the CLI says so.

Options (.ample/storage.json, also in the Storage page)

Option Default Meaning
softLimitGb 10 size above which a clean-up is suggested
keepSuperseded 0 older takes of each block that stay besides the current one
keepMinutes 60 takes younger than this are never cleaned up
archivePath none a clean-up moves the data here instead of deleting it
dataPath none the takebank on another drive
intermediates compressed compressed or wav: how new WAV takes are stored
silenceRuns true configured in the file; the current renderer does not read this option (F2)

Smaller takes

  • New WAV takes (64 KB and up) are stored compressed: a lossless container (16 bit byte planes + Brotli). The decoded bytes are exactly the bytes that were rendered, so the content address, plan ids and take ids do not change, and silence and quiet passages shrink to almost nothing; a measured sample of a real project went from 303 MB to 89 MB (29 percent).
  • Takes made before this stay plain until you run Projects, Storage, Compress the existing takes (or ample storage compress): lossless, each file is decoded and rehashed before it replaces the plain one.
  • The option intermediates (compressed default, or wav) turns it off for new data. The same data is stored once whatever it is called (content addressing); the overview counts take rows that share data.

The takebank on another drive

ample storage move D:\ample-takes\song (or the Storage page) moves the take data there with progress and sets the dataPath option; ample storage move - moves it back. New data goes to the new place at once, reads look in both places while it moves, and a stopped move continues when run again. When the folder is not reachable (an unplugged drive) a write says so (AMP5603) and what is missing renders again.

Estimate and disk check before a build

  • GET /api/build/estimate?path= (and the first line of every full build in the build log) says how many blocks have to render, about how many GB they will store and how long it takes. At first this is an educated guess from the length of the song (a stereo WAV per block; light blocks fast, GM, plugin and AI blocks slow); after each finished build the per-type size and render pace are updated with an exponentially weighted average (alpha 0.3) in .ample/analysis/build-stats.json, so the next estimate says "from N earlier builds". The stats are per project, not per machine.
  • A build of more than 2 GB asks first. A build that does not fit on the drive of the takebank (the estimate plus 20 percent) is refused before anything is written (AMP5604) with what a clean-up could give back; small builds skip the check.
  • The build log reports the progress with an estimate of the time to go.

Errors

A full disk gives AMP5600 ("not enough free space on the drive of the takebank") and an unwritable store AMP5601, with the block named, instead of a bare I/O error.

Clean-up safety rules (audit 2026-10-20)

  • Anything the clean-up cannot read (a source file, a history revision, a file in .ample, storage.json) stops the plan with AMP5606 and nothing is removed; it never guesses "nothing there".
  • Protected as well: take ids written in any file of any history revision (also of dropped lines), in finals, in assistant proposals and sessions under .ample, in sources of any size, and every id written anywhere in a plan (inputs).
  • The archive folder must be separate from the take data folder (AMP5603). ample storage move only moves take data files (64-digit hex names in two-digit folders), refuses a destination inside or around the old folder, verifies each copy byte for byte before deleting the source, and never deletes a file that is its own copy.
  • Temporary files: only direct children of .ample/tmp and .ample/ai/work|validate|audio, untouched for a day (newest file inside counts), never through a link, and never the folder of an AI task that is not yet applied, rejected or cancelled.
  • Not protected on purpose: the AMPLE Redux journal (.ample/blackbox) is not read; its sources come back through the history revisions. A build running at the same moment is covered by the one-hour window, not by a lock.

Finals: several deliverables of one song

Status (2026-10-11): built (studio, API). A ample finals command is not built yet.

A song can deliver several finals: the full version, an edit, a teaser. Everyday building does not make them; Render does, on purpose, and says first how big and how long it will be (the estimate of Storage).

What a final is

name, the first bar, how many bars (0 keeps everything to the end), a fade in (beats), a fade out (bars) and the format (mp3 or wav). A song without any has one implicit final, full (the whole song). Finals are kept per song in .ample/finals.json.

The API accepts names of 1–60 ASCII letters, digits, spaces, - and _; fromBar is clamped to 1–100000, bars to 0–100000, and each fade to 0–64. wav selects WAV; other or omitted format values use the MP3 default. Listing returns each definition with its last rendered take id, path, time and byte size when available.

Rendering one

Projects, Finals (or POST /api/finals/render): the estimate and the disk check first (AMP5604 when it does not fit), then the build of the song, then the kept bars of the master with their fades, exported to renders/<song>-<final>.<format>. The master take is recorded with the final, so a clean-up never removes it. An unknown final is AMP5605.

API

GET /api/finals?song=, POST /api/finals (add or change), POST /api/finals/delete, POST /api/finals/render.

Local server and API

Status (2026-10-03): built in chunk 70. The web UI (chunks 75 to 77) is the first client; the reference of every route is generated from docs/api/openapi.json and appears under "Local API" in this help.

ample serve starts one local web server for one project. It serves the web UI, the help and the API, and it is the only way the UI touches the engine: everything the CLI can do is a route here, and every state change goes through the command bus, so AMPLE Redux keeps its recovery record.

Starting it

ample serve --project <folder> [--port N] [--no-browser] [--allow-lan] [--root <ample folder>]
ample serve --openapi docs/api/openapi.json     # writes the OpenAPI document and exits
