  • Not done: the node editor does not draw a module instance as a node (the source editor shows it), a module cannot move its blocks on the timeline, and there is no sharing or catalog of modules (out of scope).

Quality checks

ample check quality [--take id] measures the newest take of every block that has audio (or one take) and applies the rules of spec/quality-rules.json:

Rule What Default limit
Q001 clipping runs of three or more full-scale samples none allowed
Q002 true peak 4x oversampled peak -1 dBTP
Q003 loudness integrated loudness (ITU-R BS.1770-4, gated) of the master -14 LUFS within 1.5 LU
Q004 silence longest quiet stretch inside the song (lead-in and tail excluded) 2 s
Q005 DC offset mean value 0.01
Q006 sample rate a final take not at 44100 Hz (previews are not checked) -
Q007 tempo and key fit needs an analysis plugin; reported as "not run" until then -

Results are kept per take in .ample/quality/<take>.json (derived data, easy to make again). They are advisory. .ample/quality.json can set the target and tolerance, thresholds per rule, switch rules off and name the rules that must pass before a tag or a promote ({"require":{"tag":["Q001","Q002"],"promote":["Q001"]}}); then the newest take of the master block is measured at that moment and a failure stops the tag or promote with AMP5333.

Limits: only 16-bit PCM WAV (mono or stereo, mixed down) is measured; the true peak uses a cubic interpolation, not the 48-tap filter of the standard; there is no UI for the results yet (the data is in the files and the command output).

Credits

ample credits [--format md|json] [--out file] [--write] makes the credit sheet from the plans of the newest takes (plugin, version, voice, toolprint), the modules and the library assets that the songs use (with licence and credit as kept in the library), and the people in .ample/credits.json ({"usage":"commercial","people":[{"name":"...","role":"words","note":""}]}). Licence warnings (AMP5332): a non-commercial asset when the project has a release (a tag, or usage commercial), a no-derivatives asset, an asset without a licence. Advisory, not legal advice. --write keeps the sheet in .ample/credits/; ample export and the server's export refresh it first, so every export carries a sheet made from what was really used.

Analysis

Tempo, key, loudness, spectrum, pitch and melody analysers and the analysis plugin contract are in Analysis. They are plugins by design (never in the core) and are not wired into the quality rules yet.

AMPLE Redux journal

Status (2026-10-18): AR record references, durable sequence allocation, bounded read-only search (including the Codex MCP tool), redacted assistant-task archives, opt-in session conversation capture, independent browser recovery drafts, project history preview and explicit retention controls are implemented. The History tab also exposes the open song or nested module's browser undo/redo states: preview is read-only, double-click confirms restore, Ctrl-double-click restores directly, and AR badges appear only for an exact text hash found in a durable pre-image record. Checkpoint preflights all source drafts and saves every matching dirty song/module work buffer before creating one snapshot. Existing projects continue using .ample/blackbox/ on disk for compatibility.

The journal and the Always rule

1. The idea

The history (lines, revisions, tags) holds the moments the producer chose to keep. AMPLE Redux is the append-only recovery journal underneath it. It records durable project changes and assistant-task artifacts so work can be inspected and recovered after a crash, a bad replace, a deleted block, a seed overwritten or an undo that went too far.

It is the second half of the Always rule (Decisions): the Always rule says a take never exists without its plan; AMPLE Redux says no change exists without a trace.

2. How it differs from the other layers

Layer Who decides Granularity Lives Shown
Editor undo/redo automatic, per open song or nested module one edit step; text and undo/redo stack are recoverable from this browser browser recovery buffer, offered when that file is opened after restart; the recovery diff can preselect restore or saved version for other files yes: Undo/Redo controls and the Edit history timeline
Automatic checkpoints (auto/...) automatic, before risky moves one per move, promote, update, migration in the history hidden by default
History (lines, revisions, tags, checkpoints) the producer one per Save the project, kept forever (until cleanup or purge) yes
AMPLE Redux automatic, always each durable record has an AR reference .ample/blackbox/ (compatibility path) recovery and read-only inspection

AR references (implemented)

Every journal record has a monotonic sequence and two representations: the canonical, copyable form AR-0000000000000001 and the compact UI form AR-1. IDs contain no date or suffix; timestamps are stored separately in UTC. The sequence high-water mark is persisted before appending a record, so a failed append may leave a gap but cannot make that number available again. The maximum sequence is 9,999,999,999,999,999. AMPLE's project writer lock remains the single-writer boundary; multiple read-only viewers can inspect the same archive.

3. What is recorded

Everything that changes the working copy or the project:

  • Text and structure: edits to .amplet and the other text files, block additions, deletions and moves, parameter changes, links, groups, the layout.
  • Seeds, freeze levels and plans: every seed change (with the old value), freezing and unfreezing, picked variants.
  • Time and placement: arrangement edits.
  • Library: replace, rename, relocate, copy, remove (with the full before state).
  • Settings: project, plugin and (non-secret) module settings.
  • Renders: every build start and finish, which take hash it made, and its plan (already stored by the Always rule).
  • Deletions: the full content that was deleted, not only the fact that it was.
  • History operations: go, promote, fork, drop, cleanup, tag and checkpoint moves (they are in the operation log too; the journal keeps the same facts in time order with everything else). Never recorded: secret values (only the name and version of a credential, as everywhere else), transient keystrokes before save, and audio (takes live in the take bank; the journal only holds their hashes). The Edit history timeline can therefore show an AR badge only when the whole file-text state exactly matches a durable song or module pre-image stored in Redux; the lookup pages through the journal and an unrecorded browser-only step has no AR badge.

4. Format

  • Append-only entries in segment files (or a table): id, time, who, session, group id (one user action, such as "replace kit/tape by kit/808", is one group), kind, target (block id, file, setting), before and after (a small patch, or a content hash for bigger things), and a hash of the previous entry (a chain, so tampering and gaps are detectable).
  • Crash-safe: each entry is flushed before the change is reported done; a torn last entry is detected and ignored on the next start.
  • Snapshots: every N minutes or K entries a full snapshot of the working copy (a cheap one: file hashes and the text), so restoring a moment does not mean replaying everything from the beginning.
  • Small: text patches are tiny; the big things (takes, imports, baked data) are referenced by hash. A heavy week is expected to stay in the tens of megabytes (an estimate to measure, not a measurement).

4b. A separate store inside .ample/, built to survive when things go wrong

AMPLE Redux is its own store, not a table in history.db: it currently uses the compatible storage path .ample/blackbox/. If the history database is corrupted, AMPLE Redux is not; if Redux has a problem, the history is not. Bias: better too much than too little.

.ample/blackbox/
  README.txt            how to read this folder without AMPLE (plain text, always rewritten on open)
  MANIFEST              segment list, sizes, hashes and the head of the chain; rewritten atomically, MANIFEST.prev kept
  current.log           the open segment (append-only, flushed before a change counts as done)
  seg-000123.log.zst    sealed segments (compressed, checksummed, never edited again)
  snapshots/            periodic full copies of the small important files (song, lyrics, lock, project.json, links, assets, plugins.lock)
  db-backups/           a rolling daily copy of history.db (7 kept)
  damaged/              anything that failed a check is moved here, never deleted
  • Self-describing and simple: JSON lines, each entry framed with a magic marker, a length and a CRC, plus the hash of the previous entry. A person (or a 50-line script) can read it; a damaged entry can be skipped because the next marker resynchronises the reader.
  • Write-ahead, fail closed for dangerous changes: the entry is written and flushed before the change is applied. If the write fails (disk full, permissions), destructive changes are refused (delete, replace, purge, cleanup, migrate) with a clear message; trivial edits continue but a persistent red notice says AMPLE Redux is not recording.
  • Capture generously: both before and after values (not only patches) for anything small; the raw command and its inputs, so a later bug in AMPLE cannot hide what was asked; a snapshot every 5 minutes while working, and always before a dangerous act, an upgrade or a migration; the content of everything deleted.
  • A second copy: sealed segments and snapshots are also copied to a mirror outside the project folder (<Home>/blackbox-mirror/<project uuid>/), so deleting or overwriting the project folder does not take AMPLE Redux with it. On by default, can be turned off, and says where it is.
  • Integrity checks: on open the tail is verified (a torn last entry is cut off, the bytes kept in damaged/); ample blackbox verify checks every CRC, the whole hash chain and the manifest; ample blackbox salvage reads what can be read past a damaged part.
  • Not tied to the clock: each entry has a sequence number, the wall-clock time and a monotonic time, so a clock jump or a time-zone change cannot reorder history.
  • One writer, many readers: a single writer per project (the instance lock); recovery tools and scripts read without a lock.
  • Permissions: owner-only files. Not encrypted by default; optional encryption at rest (records and mirror sealed with AES-256-GCM) is built, see Security. Never put .ample/blackbox/ in a cloud-synced folder (the health check warns).
  • Protected by AMPLE itself: nothing inside its retention window is deleted by AMPLE; "Delete project" lists its size in the dry run; a restore from a complete backup brings it back.

What can go wrong, and what saves you

Situation What happens
Crash or power loss while writing the torn last entry is detected and set aside; everything before it is intact; unsaved changes are offered back
Disk full destructive changes are refused; red notice for the rest; nothing is silently lost
history.db corrupted AMPLE Redux is separate; restore a daily db copy from db-backups/ or rebuild the working copy from snapshots plus entries
Project folder deleted or overwritten the mirror in Home has the segments and snapshots
A bug in a new AMPLE version corrupts data the raw commands and before-values are in AMPLE Redux; the snapshot taken before the upgrade is the way back
.ample/blackbox/ deleted by accident the mirror; and the health check shows "AMPLE Redux archive missing" at the next open
Cloud-sync conflict copies detected by the manifest chain; the health check warns and keeps both copies
Clock jump sequence numbers keep the order; the jump itself is recorded
Power loss while sealing a segment sealing is write-to-temp then rename; the open segment stays valid until the rename succeeds

5. Recovery (the only place it shows)

Hidden from the normal screens; reachable from Health, AMPLE Redux (advanced) and ample recover:

  • Timeline of groups ("12:41 replaced kit/tape by kit/808", "12:43 deleted block bass2", "12:47 seed of chorus_vox changed") with search ("everything that touched chorus_vox's seed", "everything deleted today") and filters by block, kind and time.
  • Restore a part, not the world: a block, a file, a parameter, a seed, a placement or a setting as it was at a chosen moment, into the working copy as an unsaved change (so it can be reviewed, saved or undone), or as a new line from that state.
  • Preview what a moment looked like (read-only, like peek) and compare it with now.
  • Automatic nudges: after a crash ("recovered N unsaved changes"), after a mass change ("12 blocks removed: recoverable from AMPLE Redux for 90 days") and when a dangerous act finishes, so the producer knows the net is there without having to think about it.
  • The journal is read-only history of the working copy: recovering never edits it, it only adds new entries.

6. Retention and cleanup (later, deliberately)

A policy, shown once in the project settings and the Health panel, adjustable: | Age | Kept | | --- | --- | | first 90 days (default) | every entry, and never thinned during the last 7 days | | 90 days to 1 year | one snapshot per hour plus every entry of a group that deleted or replaced something (their content is kept the longest) | | older than 1 year | only what a revision, tag, checkpoint or release refers to, and the deletions' content | Also a size budget (default 10 GB, adjustable): a warning at 80%, and only then is the oldest detail thinned. The defaults err on the side of keeping too much.

  • Takes are pinned by the journal. A take or baked block that the journal still refers to is not removed by gc or cleanup until its journal entries expire. That also rescues the variant you liked but did not pick.
  • Cleaning it up is a dangerous act when done by hand (ample journal prune --older-than 14d): dry run, impact, backup suggestion, typed acceptance, tombstone. The automatic thinning follows the policy and is logged.
  • Backups and exports: the journal is only in the complete backup profile and never in a partial export by default (it contains deleted content). A restore says whether a journal came along.

7. Privacy and safety

  • The journal holds deleted text (lyrics, notes) and old settings. It is local, in .ample/, never sent anywhere, excluded from sharing, and part of the "what would be lost" dry run when a project is deleted.
  • Secrets never enter it (see Project management); a credential change appears as "credential X rotated to version 3".
  • Because it is hidden, the first run tells the producer once that it exists, what it keeps and for how long, and where to turn it off or shorten it.

8. Testing

  • Replay test: replaying the journal from a snapshot must reproduce the working copy exactly, at random moments.
  • Crash test: kill the process at random points while changing things; the journal and the project must agree after restart.
  • Fuzz: random sequences of edits, deletions and replaces, with random restores, never lose data that the journal still holds.
  • Budget: writing an entry stays under a stated time per edit, so it is never felt.

9. Build order

It is a thin layer if the core is built around commands that change state (every change goes through one function that also writes the journal entry). So: the journal writer comes with the core (the same step as the history and the take bank), recovery tools come later.

10. Open questions

The original journal UI/recovery questions are resolved by AMPLE Redux (chunk 101): the user-facing name is AMPLE Redux; retention is a configurable size budget with warnings and explicit, previewed compaction; browser drafts cover multiple files; and the history view supports read-only visual preview and return to the exact current editor state. Encryption remains off by default, with optional encryption documented in Security.

Backup and restore

Status: the backup store, the archive (export and import), restore, prune, the CLI and API, and encrypted backups are built; the backup screens are not (see "As built" at the end). The rest of this page is the design the feature started from (profiles, release bundles); where the built version differs, "As built" says so.

ample backup produces one zip. ample restore puts it back into a new folder (never overwrites). The sections before "As built" are design notes; "As built" says what exists.

What is inside

my-song-backup-2026-10-02T1015.zip
├─ BACKUP-MANIFEST.json        # backup id, ample version, profile, time, machine; sha256 per file; one root hash
├─ RESTORE.md                  # plain-language instructions (readable without AMPLE)
├─ project/                    # sources (small)
│  ├─ song.amplet  ample.lock  rules/  cuts/  credits/  lyrics/  chords/  midi/
│  └─ .ample-project.json      # name, master seed, format version
├─ store/
│  ├─ history.db               # consistent copy of the SQLite history (VACUUM INTO)
│  └─ cas/ab/cd/<hash>...      # frozen audio and stems by hash (the big things)
├─ releases/   v1.release  v1.1-tweak.release  club-remix.release  [v1.bundle if the git mirror is on]
├─ snapshots/  v1.snapshot     # full inventory with all hashes and toolprints
├─ ledger/     ledger.jsonl    # hash chain of releases (+ last hash stored separately)
├─ takes/      bank.json  pinned/...
├─ tools/      registry/ (manifests, toolprints, certificates, verification history)  store/ (full profile, license permitting)
├─ packs/                      # soundsets (full profile, with license info)
├─ exports/    v1/ master.flac  stems/
├─ external/   copied/...  MISSING.txt
├─ secrets/                    # only when chosen, see below
│  ├─ secrets.enc              # encrypted bundle of the selected secrets
│  └─ SECRETS-README.txt       # what this is; there is NO password recovery
└─ meta/
   ├─ environment.json         # OS, GPU, driver, ample version
   ├─ models.lock              # hashes of used models (the models themselves are not included)
   ├─ secrets-index.json       # names and where they are used (never values)
   └─ EXCLUDED.txt             # what was left out on purpose, and why

Profiles

Profile Contents Rough size
minimal sources, lock, snapshots, ledger, take metadata KB to a few MB
standard + pinned takes, releases, exports tens of MB
complete + all takes, tool binaries, packs, copied external files GB

Choose what to export in a checklist (also saved as a named profile): sources, takes, releases, assets, tools, packs, credits with contact details, and each secret separately.

Secrets

Secrets live in a vault outside the project (OS key store; on Linux an encrypted file). The project refers to them by name (secret:weather_api). Only secrets you declare count (tokens, passwords, private keys, URLs with tokens), never your whole environment.

Choice Result
Secrets inside (suggested default) secrets/secrets.enc in the zip, encrypted with your master passphrase. The rest may stay readable, or everything can be encrypted (--encrypt all).
Secrets in a sibling file my-song-backup-....secrets.enc next to the zip, same backup id. Store it elsewhere (password manager, other disk).
No secrets names and usage only, no values

The release signing key is off by default and must be ticked on purpose, with a warning: whoever holds it can sign in your name.

Encryption

  • Envelope: a random data key encrypts the secrets (AES-256-GCM or XChaCha20-Poly1305, authenticated); that key is wrapped with a key derived from the passphrase (memory-hard, e.g. Argon2id, parameters stored in the header).
  • No password recovery. Lose the passphrase and the secrets are gone. Optional recovery key: a random key shown once (words or QR) and stored offline.
  • The manifest hashes the ciphertext, never a plaintext secret (a hash of a weak secret can be brute-forced).
  • Prefer an existing, reviewed format (the age format, passphrase or public keys) over a home-made one, if a good library exists.
  • Honest trade-off: secrets inside the same file as the data is convenient, but whoever has the zip and the passphrase has everything. The sibling file splits that knowledge. When "inside" is chosen the tool prints one line: "Secrets are in this file, encrypted. Keep them separate instead?"

Restore without retyping

$ ample restore my-song-backup.zip
  Passphrase: ****     -> 4 secrets restored   tested: weather_api ok, remote_token ok
  Missing (not in the backup): ftp_pw    -> [fill in now] [later]
  • One passphrase, then all secrets go back into the local vault automatically (re-protected for the new machine; machine-bound secrets cannot be copied raw, which is why they are exported into the encrypted bundle).
  • Anything missing appears in one screen: the name, where it is used, and a test button.
  • If the sibling file is absent, everything else is restored and only that list is asked for.

Checks

  • ample backup verify file.zip compares every file with the manifest and the root hash without unpacking into a project.
  • Reproducible zip: sorted entries, fixed timestamps, so identical content gives an identical zip hash.
  • Audio (FLAC) is stored without extra compression; above 4 GB use Zip64 or a split backup.
  • ample restore --verify checks all hashes after restoring and reports what is missing or not reproducible (frozen-only without a copy).

Not included (also listed in meta/EXCLUDED.txt)

Caches and temp files, logs, big models (hash only), drivers and system files (recorded as environment), and by default the full take bank in standard.

As built

Where: Ample.Core/Backup (BackupStore, Archive, PruneBackupsAct, RestoreInPlaceAct, BackupPolicy), the CLI ample backup create|list|verify|prune|policy, ample export, ample import, ample restore, and the API routes /api/backup*, /api/export, /api/acts/prune-backups, /api/acts/restore-in-place (the health view also shows the last backup).

The backup store (a folder you choose)

<target>/objects/ab/abcdef...     one file per distinct content (name = sha256), written atomically (.part then rename)
<target>/backups/<id>.json        one manifest per backup, immutable, written last
<target>/verified.json            which backups passed a verify (the "last good" record)
  • Incremental by content: a second backup stores only the files whose content is new; an unchanged project stores nothing (0 new files in the tests).
  • What goes in: every file of the project except .ample/locks, .ample/tmp, .ample/backups, .ample/vault*, *.secret, *.tmp and the SQLite journals. history.db is copied with the SQLite backup API, so the copy is consistent while the project is open. --no-takes leaves out .ample/takes and .ample/data.
  • Manifest (format 1): id (time and the start of the entry hash), project id and name, time, whether takes are included, and per file path, hash and size.
  • Resumable: an interrupted backup leaves only objects (and .part files); the next run reuses them and writes the manifest. Left-over temp folders are cleaned after an hour.
  • Space: the free space of the target is checked before anything is written (AMP5300).
  • Verify rehashes every stored file (missing and damaged ones are listed) and, when clean, records the backup as the last good one. Restore copies each file through a hash check and refuses damaged data; it goes into a new folder (AMP5301 if it is not empty).
  • Prune (--keep N, --daily D) is a dangerous act with a dry run; the newest backup and the last good one are always kept; files that no kept backup uses are removed.
  • In-place restore is a dangerous act: files are replaced or added, files that are not in the backup are moved to .ample/tmp/restore-trash-* (never deleted), the history comes back as it was. Close other programs that use the project first.
  • Before dangerous acts: ample backup policy --target <folder> --auto on (or /api/backup/policy) makes a backup before every dangerous act the server runs; a failing backup stops the act (AMP5305). The dry run of every act can tell how old the last backup is (BackupPolicy.Suggestion).

The archive (export and import)

One zip file (any zip tool reads it): manifest.json and files/<path>. The manifest is { "format": 1, "tool": "ample", "projectId", "projectName", "created", "includesTakes", "entries": [ { "path", "hash": "sha256:...", "size" } ] }. ample import checks every hash while extracting into a new folder (AMP5302, and nothing is left behind), refuses a folder that is not empty, rejects paths that leave the folder, and with --new-id gives the project a new id (the default keeps the id). Secrets and locks are never exported.

Measured (2026-10-03, Windows 11, Debug build, one machine)

A project of 40 MB of audio and a few small files: create 209 ms (191 MB/s), verify 193 ms, restore 208 ms.

Not built (and where)

Backup profiles (minimal, standard, complete) and the checklist of what to include (only takes in or out), secrets bundles, release bundles and the git mirror, remote targets, scheduled backups (only "before a dangerous act"), point-in-time restore from AMPLE Redux pre-images, RESTORE.md inside the backup, and the backup screens.

Encrypted projects (as built)

When a project is encrypted (Security), every object a backup stores is sealed (AES-256-GCM, frames of 1 MiB) and the backup folder gets a copy of the wrapped key as encryption.json (never the passphrase); verify and restore open the objects with the passphrase from AMPLE_PASSPHRASE. A folder that holds the key of one project refuses another project's key (AMP5314). Exports stay plain zip files; only their black-box segments stay sealed. Backups never contain the vault (vault.json lives in the library folder, outside every project).

Security: the vault, signing and optional encryption

Status (2026-10-03): built in chunk 92. This page says what is protected, what is not, and how to use it.

What is built

Part What it does Where
Vault Secrets (API keys, tokens) live in one file of your library folder (vault.json), sealed with a key made from a passphrase. Projects and plugin manifests only carry the name of a secret. A plugin gets only the secrets its manifest declares, as environment variables, and the value is redacted from its captured logs. ample vault set|list|remove, Ample.Storage.Security.PassphraseVault, Ample.Plugins.VaultSecretProvider
Signing You sign the newest record of a project's black box (or a file such as an export) with your own key. ample verify checks the hash chain and every signature: a changed record, a cut-off journal, a forged signature log or an unknown signer is reported (AMP5312). ample keys generate|list|export|rotate, ample sign, ample verify
Encryption at rest (optional, off by default) Every record of the black box (and its mirror in your home folder) is sealed; backups made from then on are sealed file by file. A data key is wrapped by your passphrase; changing the passphrase re-wraps the key and re-encrypts nothing. ample encrypt status|enable|disable|recovery-kit|passphrase

Passphrases and secret values are never arguments (they would show in process lists and shell history): they come from environment variables (AMPLE_VAULT_PASSPHRASE, AMPLE_PASSPHRASE, AMPLE_NEW_PASSPHRASE) or from standard input (echo the-secret | ample vault set NAME).

Cryptography used (no custom primitives)

Need Choice Why
Sealing AES-256-GCM (.NET AesGcm), random 96-bit nonce per record and per 1 MiB file frame Authenticated; part of the platform. XChaCha20-Poly1305 would need an extra library.
Passphrase to key PBKDF2-HMAC-SHA256, 600 000 iterations, random salt Part of the platform. Argon2id (memory-hard) would be better against GPUs but needs an extra library; revisit.
Signatures ECDSA P-256 with SHA-256 (.NET ECDsa), IEEE P1363 format The platform has no Ed25519.
Random RandomNumberGenerator Operating system source.

The threat model

Protected

  • A stolen laptop, a copied project folder or a backup drive in the wrong hands cannot show the black box (what was deleted, replaced or written, with the pre-images) without the passphrase, when encryption is on. Neither can the encrypted backup objects.
  • A secret never reaches a project file, a journal record, a backup or an export: commands carry the secret's name, never its value, and the vault file keeps values sealed. A canary-secret test scans the project, the black box, a backup and an export.
  • Tampering with the black box shows: every record carries the hash of the one before it (and a checksum), a signed head ties the chain to a key of yours, and AES-GCM refuses a changed sealed record.

Not protected

  • Anyone who has the passphrase, or the unlocked process, sees everything. While the program runs the key is in memory.
  • The song, lyrics, notes, the history database and the takes in the project folder are not encrypted (they are the work you share and the files other tools read). Use your system's disk encryption (BitLocker, FileVault, LUKS) for those.
  • Exports are plain zip files by design: they are meant to be shared. Their black-box segments stay sealed, so the receiver needs the passphrase for those only.
  • File names, sizes and the hash of each backed-up file are visible in the backup manifest (the objects are named by the hash of their plain content, so someone who already has a file can tell that it is in the backup).
  • The hourly summaries that thinning leaves of old black-box segments (hour, kind, count) are not sealed.
  • A signature proves that a key signed a head at some time and that the journal still contains that record unchanged. It does not prove when (the time is the signer's clock) or who holds the key.
  • Signatures of records that thinning later removed cannot be checked any more (they are listed as "no longer checkable", not as a problem).
  • A malicious process running as you can read the vault passphrase from the environment. The vault protects against theft of files, not against malware on a running machine.

Key loss

  • Lost passphrase and no recovery kit: the sealed black box and the sealed backups cannot be opened by anyone, including us. There is no back door. The song itself is not sealed and stays usable.
  • ample encrypt enable is a dangerous act: the dry run says this in plain words, and you must type encrypt this project and give a reason.
  • ample encrypt recovery-kit --out file writes a text file with the data key itself and the key settings. Keep it offline (paper or a drive in a drawer). Whoever holds it can open the sealed data without the passphrase, so it is as secret as the passphrase.
  • ample encrypt disable (also a dangerous act) writes the black box in the clear again. Backups made while it was on stay sealed; their folder keeps a copy of the wrapped key, so the passphrase still opens them.
  • A backup folder holds the key of one project: backing up a second project with another key into the same folder is refused (AMP5314).

How it works

  • .ample/encryption.json holds the format, the KDF settings, the data key sealed by the passphrase-derived key, and an HMAC key check. It holds no secret by itself.
  • A sealed black-box line is enc1: plus base64 of nonce, tag and ciphertext of the plain line; the hash chain and the checksum are over the plain lines, so verification works the same with or without encryption, and plain and sealed lines may be mixed (the switch is crash-safe). The journal opens the key from the passphrase source (the environment) and refuses to open an encrypted project without it (AMP5310).
  • A sealed backup object starts with AMPLEENC1\n, then frames of up to 1 MiB, each with its own nonce and tag.
  • Signatures are lines of .ample/signatures.jsonl: key id, public key, the sequence number and line hash of the signed record, the time and the signature over ample-sig1|project id|seq|hash|time. File signatures are <file>.sig.
  • Key rotation retires the active signing key (its private half is deleted) and makes a new one; retired keys keep verifying.

Not built (see the plan)

  • The operating system credential stores (Windows Credential Manager/DPAPI, Keychain, libsecret) are not used: the vault is a passphrase-sealed file on every system.
  • No UI yet for the vault, keys or encryption (the web UI shows nothing of it); everything is on the command line.
  • The data key is not rotated (only the passphrase). Re-encrypting with a new key means disabling and enabling again.
  • Secrets in a backup bundle (secrets.enc), a sibling secrets file and "restore without retyping" from the backup design are not built; backups simply never contain the vault.
  • Argon2id and XChaCha20-Poly1305 (see above).

Analysis

Status: built; it includes a project-scoped review of audio transcriptions. Analysis lives outside the core, in Ample.Plugins, and never changes a take.

What is there

Analyser Result Method Tolerance measured on synthetic fixtures
tempo BPM, confidence, beat grid onset strength (positive energy change) and autocorrelation, shortest strong lag, parabolic refinement within 1 BPM for clean click tracks from 70 to 180 BPM
key key (tonic and mode), confidence, chroma, three candidates chroma from an FFT and the Krumhansl-Kessler profiles right key for the C major, E major and A minor chord sequences of the tests; the relative key is the usual confusion
loudness integrated, momentary max, short-term max, loudness range, true peak EBU R128 (ITU-R BS.1770-4 K-weighting, gates at -70 LUFS and -10 LU; range after EBU Tech 3342) 0.3 LU for a steady sine; a range of two levels 15 LU apart is found within 2 LU
spectrum centroid, 85 % roll-off, flatness, shares of four bands averaged Hann-windowed FFT frames a sine puts its centroid near its pitch; white noise has flatness above 0.5
pitch pitch contour every 10 ms with a confidence YIN (difference function, cumulative mean normalisation, absolute threshold 0.15, parabolic interpolation) within 10 cents for tones from 110 to 880 Hz, also with 20 cents of vibrato
melody melody plan: notes (pitch, start and length in beats on a quarter-beat grid, bar) segmentation of the pitch contour; the tempo comes from the option {"tempo":BPM}, else from the tempo analyser, else 120 a synthesised five-note melody with a rest comes back as the same pitches on the same beats

These tolerances are measured on synthetic signals only. Nothing is claimed for real recordings until they are measured on real songs. pYIN (a probabilistic layer over YIN that copes better with real voices) needs a library or a Python plugin; the choice for now is plain YIN, recorded here so that it can be replaced behind the same schema.

Results, schemas and caching

  • Every result must fit spec/schema/analysis-<kind>.schema.json (the same small schema subset as the other spec schemas); a result that does not is refused (AMP5343).
  • ample analyze <take> --with <analyser> [--options json] stores the result in .ample/analysis/<key>.json and links it to the take in .ample/analysis/index.json. The key is a hash of the audio content, the analyser id, its version and the sorted options, so the same audio is analysed once, a new analyser version recomputes, and two takes with the same audio share a result. ample analyze --list lists the analysers.
  • The results are not stored as take data: the take bank counts data that no take owns as orphans and would quarantine them. A take, its plan and its data are never touched.
  • Analysers are pure: the same samples and options always give the same text (tested).

The melody plan and re-sing

The melody analyser writes {"schema":"ample-melody/1","tempo":T,"notes":[{"pitch":60,"start":0,"length":1,"bar":1,...}]}. Stored as data with the role melody of a take and pinned with freeze plan, it reaches the plugin as the input melody (see Controllability); the engine records its data id in the plan. A test builds a plan from a synthesised melody and feeds it through freeze plan into the echo test plugin. What a real model does with it (a re-sing that keeps the notes) depends on the plugin and is not claimed.

Analysis plugins (the contract)

A plugin of kind analysis lists the analyses it offers in analyses (its blocks may be empty) and answers the request analyze with { "jobDir", "analysis", "input": "in/audio.wav", "options" } by { "result": { ... } }. The host copies the take's audio into the job folder, checks the result against the schema and returns it (AMP5343, AMP5344). For file-producing analyses such as source separation, the response may also include outputs: [{ "role": "vocals", "path": "out/vocals.wav" }]; paths are relative to the private job folder and are rejected when missing, duplicated, outside the folder or oversized (AMP5272, AMP5274). plugins/analysis-fake exercises this contract with generated bytes. A real separation/transcription plugin is not bundled.

Permission: a plugin whose manifest needs the GPU or the network is never started unless the user says yes to the question the host asks (--allow-gpu, --allow-network on the command line; AMP5340 otherwise). The built-in analysers use neither.

Not built

  • The optional analysis-local-transcription plugin uses preinstalled Audio Separator and Basic Pitch packages, plus a user-selected, preinstalled separator model. Model weights and Python packages are not bundled or downloaded; network access is blocked. The compute-device choice defaults to GPU, with a CPU option, and GPU jobs require explicit permission. Configure its Python executable, complete local model folder and model filename in the transcription wizard's JSON options. See plugins. Real-model accuracy and runtime have not been measured here.
  • The UI uploads at most 10 minutes/128 MiB, shows progress, synchronized stem playback, a 16-bit WAV waveform and up to 8 MiB of returned vocal pitch/model-activity metadata, and keeps results under .ample/transcriptions/.
  • The review UI groups vocal pitch frames above a model-activity threshold into editable note estimates and can download them or import them as a MIDI source block. The local Basic Pitch adapter's displayed 0–1 value is the clamped note amplitude, not calibrated confidence or a probability. When the selected separator returns multiple accompaniment stems, the adapter estimates one MIDI artifact per stem and suggests an editable GM program from the stem label; it also emits a combined multitrack MIDI artifact for one-step import. A model that returns only a complete instrumental stem produces one backing estimate. Stem labels come from model filenames and are not instrument recognition. Drum stems are skipped by default because Basic Pitch does not map drum hits; the explicit drumMode: "pitched" option requests a rough pitched estimate, not a percussion map. Non-vocal MIDI artifacts can be downloaded or imported as MIDI source blocks. Raw vocal MIDI artifacts are download-only; vocal notes must be reviewed and accepted in the pitch lane before AMPLE imports them. Creating final instrument-block tracks from these estimates remains a user-reviewed conversion step.
  • The quality rule Q007 (tempo and key fit between blocks) still reports "not run": wiring the analysers into the quality rules is the next step.
  • No model weights are bundled, and pYIN is not implemented. The local model adapter reports estimates, not recovered ground truth.

Real instruments: sample drums and guitar

General MIDI tracks can also use the gm block and the licensed MuseScore General SF2 pack. Fetch the full GM bank with node tools/fetch-gm-soundfont.mjs --download; verify its pinned digest with --verify. The gm block supports project-contained SoundFonts and pack:musescore-general; converted MIDI modules use the pack alias. The SF2 renderer reads only samples selected by the requested bank, program, key and velocity zones and keeps all pitch, envelope and loop arithmetic integer-based. Modulators and SF3 are not yet supported.

Status (2026-10-03): built as part of chunk 98 follow-up. Tested in tests/Ample.Core.Tests/SamplerTests.cs (21 tests), web/lib/test/stepseq.test.mjs (the pattern grammar of the editors), web/lib/test/numfield.test.mjs (number fields) and in the browser (spec-tests/parity/samples.spec.ts for building, samples-ui.spec.ts for the editors).

The built-in drums, bass and piano are small synthesised sounds. The drums block (with a sample kit) and the guitar block play recordings that you keep in the project, and every knob stays text: the pattern, the strum, the chords, the swing.

Sample sets

A sample set is a folder of WAV files inside the project, for example samples/rusty-kit/ or samples/emily-guitar/. A block names it with kit (drums) or set (guitar); a name with a / that is a folder holding WAV files is a sample set, anything else (the built-in kit/tape, felt-piano) is the old synthesised sound.

  • Formats: 8, 16, 24 or 32-bit PCM and 32-bit float WAV, mono or stereo (mixed down), any sample rate (converted to the build rate with a fixed-point linear interpolation).
  • Where they come from: your own recordings or free ones. The demo project uses two CC0 sets by Karoryfer Samples (Swirly Drums and Emilyguitar, from the sfzinstruments collection on GitHub). Keep a samples/README.txt with the sources and licences; the credits sheet only knows what the library knows.
  • Layers and round robins on disk (2026-10-03): one flat folder stays. name.wav is layer 1, round robin 1; other files are name_v<L>_r<R>.wav (1-based, at most 3 digits, _ as separator because notes contain #; name_v2.wav and name_r2.wav alone are allowed; anything else is a plain name). NoteOf and the voice lookup read the base name. The engine still plays layer 1, round robin 1 only (a folder with extra files builds the same bytes as before), but every file is hashed into the plan, so adding one makes a new take. An optional set.json next to the WAVs (layersOffered, layersTaken, roundRobinsTaken) records what the source had and what the fetch took. GET /api/samples groups by base name and returns layers, roundRobins, offered and per voice voices; the picker says "N layers on disk, engine plays M".
  • In plans and the cache: the hash of every file of the set is part of the plan of the take (input kind sample, with the project path). Replace a sample and the block makes a new take; all other blocks stay cached. A take's plan says exactly which files made it.

Drums

drums beat at 1 for 8 {
  kit samples/rusty-kit
  pattern kick:x.......x.....x. snare:....X.......X..o hat:x.x.x.x.x.x.x.x.
  swing 12
  humanize 25
}
  • The kit folder holds one file per voice, named after the voice: kick.wav, snare.wav, hat.wav (and any other name you use in a pattern: tom.wav, crash.wav, hat-open.wav).
  • The pattern is a name (beat-A, beat-B, which still work and use kick, snare, hat) or one grid per voice, voice:steps, separated by spaces. 16 steps make a bar (12 in 3/4, or the steps of the block, see below); a shorter grid repeats inside the bar (kick:x... is four on the floor of sixteenths), a longer grid goes on over the next bars (32 steps are two bars, 48 three). x is a hit, X an accent, o a ghost note, . a rest.
  • steps (1 to 64, drums 1.5): the steps in a bar. Without it a bar has four steps for every beat (16 in 4/4, 12 in 3/4). A step lasts a bar divided by this number, so the same pattern plays at another speed whatever the tempo of the song is: steps 8 makes every step twice as long (the pattern of 16 steps now lasts two bars, at half the speed), steps 32 half as long. This is how a drum layer keeps its speed in a song of another tempo. A grid that does not fit the bars (a 20-step grid in a bar of 16) gets the warning AMP2095.
  • swing (0 to 60): how far the odd steps are pushed later, as a percentage of a step.
  • humanize (0 to 100): a little deterministic variation in volume (up to 20 %) and timing (up to 5 ms), drawn from the seed of the block: the same song always sounds the same, another seed sounds different.
  • choke (optional text, template drums 1.3): rules separated by ;, each voice:closer,closer (for example choke open:hat,pedal). A hit of a closer voice cuts the sounding hits of the first voice from that moment, with a 7 ms fade. The hits are collected first and mixed in the order they were made, so no rule gives the same bytes as before. A rule without a colon or closers fails with AMP5351.
  • step velocity (drums renderer version 4): besides x (hit), X (accent) and o (ghost) a step may be a digit 1 (softest) to 9 (loudest), for example kick:9...5...9...3.... In the studio, shift+click on a step cycles through the digits 3, 5, 7 and 9, and the velocity lane under each voice sets any digit by clicking or dragging the bars.
  • voice options in the pattern (drums renderer version 4): a voice grid shorter than 16 steps repeats (a grid of 12 steps is a bar of three beats repeated; the step editor's length box writes this). A voice grid may end with @ and options separated by commas: m mutes the voice, l<dB> sets its level (-24 to 12), p<pan> pans it (-32 left to 32 right), s<swing> gives the voice its own swing in percent (0 to 60), t<semitones> tunes the voice up or down (-24 to 24, for toms and percussion), for example kick:x...x...@l-3,p-8,s30. A pattern with any panned voice renders stereo (equal-power pan table); without pan the output stays mono. An unknown option fails with AMP5351.
  • map (optional text, template drums 1.4): replaces voices of the kit by samples of other kit folders, entries separated by ;, each voice:folder/sample (for example map kick:samples/other/kick2;snare:samples/other/clap). The mapped kit folders go into the plan of the take. A malformed entry fails with AMP5351, a sample that is not in the folder with AMP5350.
  • fallback (optional text, template drums 1.4): a kit folder used for pattern voices the kit does not have. Without it a missing voice is an error (AMP5350); with it the voice plays from the fallback kit and the build warns with AMP5256.
  • A voice that has no file, or a grid with other characters, fails the block with AMP5350 or AMP5351 and says what the folder has or what is allowed.

Named patterns and sections (2026-10-08)

A drums block (and a guitar block, for its strum) can hold several named patterns and a song that puts them in order:

drums beat at 1 for 16 {
  kit samples/rusty-kit
  pattern kick:x.......x....... snare:....x.......x... hat:x.x.x.x.x.x.x.x.
  patterns verse=kick:x...x...x...x... snare:....x.......x... hat:x.x.x.x.x.x.x.x. / fill=kick:xxxxxxxx snare:xxxxxxxx hat:xxxxxxxx
  song pattern*3 fill verse*4 fill
}
  • patterns: name=voice grids entries separated by /. Names are letters, digits, - and _; pattern, beat-A and beat-B are taken. The grids are the same as in pattern, with all voice options.
  • song: the sections in order, each a pattern name and optionally *bars (one bar when it is left out). The word pattern is the plain pattern of the block; beat-A and beat-B work too. Bar k of the block plays entry k of the sequence; the sequence repeats when the block is longer. Without song the plain pattern plays on every bar, as before.
  • A name in song that is not a pattern, a repeat that is not a whole number from 1 to 999 and a pattern defined twice are AMP5351. The built-in sound (no kit) takes patterns and song too.
  • For the guitar the entries are strums (verse=D...D.u.D.u. / fill=DdDdDdDd...) and the word pattern means the plain strum.
  • In the properties panel the grid has a pattern chooser (New, Duplicate, Rename, Delete) and a strip of sections (chips with their bars, move, remove, drag to reorder); the Patterns view (the button in the panel, the block menu) shows the lanes with the samples, the grid and the sections full width. Bass and piano have no pattern grammar of their own; they get one in the planned sequencer block.

Velocity layers

A voice or note may have several recordings for soft and hard playing. name.wav is layer 1, round robin 1; name_v<L>_r<R>.wav is layer L, round robin R (kick_v2_r1.wav, c3_v3_r1.wav). With N the highest layer number of a voice or note, a velocity v (0 to 32768) plays layer min(N-1, v*N/32769) (0 based, integer arithmetic); a layer without a file is played by the nearest layer that has one (the lower on a tie). A folder without layer files sounds exactly as before.

  • Drums: o is velocity 14000, x 26000, X 32768 (humanize changes it a little first).
  • Guitar: D 32768, U 26000, d 20000, u 16000.
  • Piano and bass: every note of the midi-clip has a MIDI velocity (1 to 127, default 96) that is scaled to 0..32768 for the layer and also scales the gain (96 is the old level). In a melody write it as a third field: c4:1:110. The bass uses the velocity of the lowest note of the bar.
  • Every layer file is hashed into the plan, so replacing kick_v2_r1.wav makes a new take.

SFZ sets (2026-10-15, Phase 1 "basis" of plan/sfz-import/README.md)

A set (not yet kit) value may name an .sfz file instead of a folder of note-named WAVs, for example set samples/karoryfer/unruly-drums.sfz. AMPLE reads the file's own opcodes instead of a filename convention, so a pack's own mapping is used as-is — no manual fetch-and-rename step is needed for a pitched instrument.

  • What is read today: <global>/<master>/<group>/<region> header inheritance, #include (verbatim, nested, relative to the including file's own folder), #define (textual substitution), sample (with default_path), lokey/hikey/key, pitch_keycenter (default: key, else lokey), lovel/hivel (0-127, scaled to AMPLE's 0-32768 velocity range the same way MIDI velocity is), tune (cents) and transpose (semitones, both rounded to AMPLE's whole-semitone Region.Tune), volume/gain (dB), seq_position (round robin position), group/off_by (SFZ03, drum kits only, see below), amp_velcurve_000..amp_velcurve_127 (a static velocity-to-amplitude table, linearly interpolated between the points given, holding the nearest point's level outside its range; applied on top of volume/gain at note time, replacing the default linear velocity response for that region only — layer/round-robin selection itself stays linear), and cutoff/fil_type/fil_veltrack (a static or velocity-tracked low-pass only: lpf_1p one stage, lpf_2p — the SFZ default when fil_type is left out — two stages in series, reusing the engine's existing integer one-pole filter; fil_veltrack (cents, -9600 to 9600) moves the cutoff at max velocity relative to velocity 0, using the same cents-to-ratio math pitch-shifting already uses; any other fil_type and resonance are kept-and-warned, no filter envelope yet).
  • Also read today (2026-10-15): lfo01_freq/lfo01_pitch/lfo01_delay (a pitch LFO, triangle wave only - forces the whole block through the per-frame expressive playback path); fileg_attack/decay/sustain/release/hold/depth (a filter envelope, same force-expressive note); trigger=release (a release-triggered companion region, see "SFZ sets and release samples" below) and, for a pitched set rendered by the piano block only, trigger=first/legato; xfin_lovel/xfin_hivel/xfout_lovel/xfout_hivel (a one-sided velocity-edge gain taper on the region RegionResolver.Choose already picked, not a true two-region crossfade); resonance (dB, an approximation - a gain bump just below the cutoff, not a true resonant filter pole); and, for a drums kit, off_time (overrides the block's choke fade) and polyphony/note_polyphony (caps simultaneous hits of one voice, first-come-first-served).
  • What is not read yet, and is kept-and-warned (AMP5394) rather than silently dropped: pan (no per-region pan field exists yet), offset/end (sample trimming), pitch_keytrack other than 100, non-low-pass filter types, trigger=first/legato for bass/guitar (see below), off_mode=normal, the <curve>-block form of curves, LFOs beyond the first/pitch-only, and every *_onccN opcode.
  • *_onccN (live MIDI CC modulation) is permanently out of scope, not "later": amplitude_onccN, cutoff_onccN, pitch_onccN and the rest exist for a live performer moving a controller while playing; AMPLE builds a song offline from a static, programmatic .amplet sequence, so there is no live CC stream at render time for these opcodes to read. They are read, kept and reported with AMP5394 like any other unread opcode — never silently dropped — so a pack that leans on them for its character is at least visible as "present but not applied." If AMPLE ever grows a live-performance mode this is worth revisiting, but it is not expected to.
  • Loops and amplitude envelopes: loop_mode=loop_continuous and loop_sustain both use AMPLE's sustain-loop playback; no_loop, one_shot and an absent mode do not loop. loop_start/loop_end are sample-native frame positions, rescaled to the build rate; an omitted end uses the whole decoded sample. loop_crossfade is in seconds. AMPLE does not distinguish continuous from sustain looping after note-off. ampeg_attack/decay/release/hold (seconds) and ampeg_sustain (percent) configure the region's integer ADSR (hold is a plateau at full level between attack and decay); an absent envelope leaves the old fixed fade. These apply to pitched set regions; filter envelopes and release-triggered samples remain open. See plan/sfz-import/README.md.
  • A kit (drums) value may also name an .sfz file (SFZ05): each region's key is mapped to a voice name through the General MIDI percussion map (36→kick, 38→snare, 42/44→hat, 46→hat-open, 49/52/55/57→crash, 51/53/59→ride, every other tom key→tom, ...) instead of becoming a pitched region — this is a real, documented standard, not a guess, but several related GM keys deliberately collapse onto one AMPLE voice name (every tom key becomes tom). A key the map does not know becomes key<N> (still addressable in a pattern, just without a friendly name) and warns (AMP5394). A region needs key/pitch_keycenter/lokey to be read at all.
  • group/off_by (SFZ03, drum kits only): every region sharing a group number is closed by a hit of any region declaring that number as its off_by — checked at region precision (SFZ12, 2026-10-16): the choke-and-fade mixing pass looks at each hit's own resolved Region.Group/Region.OffBy, so when one AMPLE voice name covers more than one region with different group membership (for example a soft, ungrouped articulation layered with a hard, grouped one on the same key), only the hit whose own region is actually in the group gets cut — not every hit of that voice name. SfzReader still also derives the older voice:closer1,closer2 text form into its result (for the documented wire format), but the drums block's own hand-written choke parameter and the SFZ-sourced region choke are now two independent checks feeding the one mixing pass, not one merged into the other. off_mode=normal is not read yet (kept-and-warned); off_time overrides the block's whole-block choke fade (see above).
  • Paths are root-jailed, one level wider than the .sfz file itself (SFZ06): every #include and sample= path must resolve inside the whole project (a project-relative set/kit value) or inside the matched pack's own folder (a pack: value) — never anywhere else on disk. This is wider than just the .sfz file's own folder tree on purpose: a real pack's programs and samples commonly sit in sibling folders (confirmed against Karoryfer's "Frankensnare", whose Programs/*.sfz reach ../Samples/...), which a same-folder-only jail would reject outright.
  • Only WAV (PCM or float) samples are read, same as a plain folder set — a real pack's samples are often FLAC; fetch-audio-packs.mjs's own ffmpeg conversion is still the only path to use a FLAC-only pack's audio with AMPLE today.
  • In plans and the cache: the .sfz file itself, every file it #includes and every sample it references are each hashed into the plan (kind: sample), exactly like every WAV of a folder-based set today — change any one of them and the block makes a new take, changing an unrelated file next to them does not.
  • A damaged or missing .sfz file, or one with no usable region, fails the block with AMP5350 (wrapping the underlying AMP5395 detail).

Per-set gain and tuning

An optional set.json in the sample folder, { "gain": -3, "tune": 1 }, evens out packs: gain is whole dB (-24 to 12) applied to every region of the set, tune is whole semitones (-24 to 24) by which the recordings sound sharp (they are played that much lower, drums included). Block parameters (gain, strum, pattern) stay as they are on top. The file is hashed into the plan (set.json as a sample input), so editing it makes a new take; a file that is not such an object fails the block with AMP5350. No file means gain 0 and tune 0, unchanged bytes.

Sustain loops and an integer envelope (S08, 2026-10-15)

set.json may also carry two optional, independent entries. Neither changes a set that does not use them: without them a region's LoopMode stays none and the note fades the same fixed way it always has.

  • loops, per base name (the same name a .wav/_v<L>_r<R>.wav or an SFZ region resolves to): { "loops": { "arco": { "start": 1000, "end": 5000, "crossfade": 200 } } }. start/end/crossfade are sample frames at the project's build rate. Playback runs the raw recording from its own start up to end; once a note needs more frames than the recording has, it wraps back to start and repeats forever, blending the last crossfade frames of each pass into the material just before start so the wrap point is not an audible click (LoopPlayer, already used standalone before this). A note shorter than the recording is unaffected — only a note that actually runs out of recorded audio ever loops.
  • envelope: one integer ADSR for the whole set, in whole milliseconds and a 0-100 sustain percentage: { "envelope": { "attack": 5, "hold": 0, "decay": 50, "sustain": 80, "release": 200 } }. Applied per note in place of the renderer's usual fixed fade (today: play the recording, then a fixed ~120 ms linear fade-out): attack ramps from silence, an optional hold plateaus at full level, decay eases to the sustain level, the note holds at sustain for as long as it is held, then release fades from wherever the envelope had reached. An explicit per-note rel= (note expression) always wins over the set's envelope for that one note — a performance override is more specific than the sample's own authored envelope.
  • Where this is wired in today: the guitar/bass/piano sampled-set note paths (PlayNote/PlayExpressiveNote, including .sfz-sourced pitched sets). The drums kit path reads the envelope since 2026-10-20 (each hit runs through the set's attack/decay/sustain/release over its own length) but never loops: a one-shot drum hit has nothing to sustain.
  • Every region's loop/envelope choice is deterministic and integer (no floating point, no real-time clock): the same song and seed render the same bytes on every machine, exactly like the rest of the sampler.

Round robins

Several files for the same voice, note and layer (kick_v1_r1.wav, kick_v1_r2.wav, ...) are different recordings of the same hit. Each hit picks one of them from its own deterministic stream: a StableRng seeded with the block seed xor a constant xor a hash of the voice name (drums: one stream per voice; guitar, piano and bass: one stream for the notes). It is a different stream from the humanize one, so the humanize timing and volume of existing takes do not change. The streams start again at every render: the same song gives the same hits on two runs and on another path, another seed gives other choices. The renderers of drums, bass, piano and guitar are version 2.

Guitar

guitar gitaar at 1 for 8 {
  set samples/emily-guitar
  strum D...D.u.D...D.u.
  voicing open
  stagger 22
  gain 0
  from chords.notes -> notes
}
  • The set folder holds recorded notes named by note: e2.wav, a2.wav, c3.wav, eb3.wav, gb3.wav, c#4.wav (C4 is middle C). A note that is not recorded is made from the nearest recording, played faster or slower (like a tape), so a set with a recording every third semitone is enough.
  • The chords come in as notes (the notes input, for example from a midi-clip). The root of each bar's chord decides the strings.
  • voicing: open (five strings: the root low, the fifth, the octave, the third above that and a high fifth), triad (root, third, fifth around middle C) or power (root, fifth, octave).
  • strum: 16 steps per bar (or the steps parameter of the block: steps 8 makes every step twice as long, so the strum plays at half speed whatever the tempo of the song is); several bars separated by | cycle by bar number. D a loud down-strum, d a soft one, U a loud up-strum, u a soft one, x mutes the strings, . lets them ring. A strum plays the strings one after the other, stagger milliseconds apart (0 to 80, default 22); an up-strum plays them in the opposite order. Strings ring until the next strum.
  • gain in dB (-24 to 12).
  • A set without note-named files, a strum with other characters or an unknown voicing fails the block with AMP5350 or AMP5351.

In the web UI

Select a drums or guitar block and the properties panel shows a step editor above the parameters (the same text parameters stay below it, and the source stays the truth):

  • Drums: a sample kit chooser (the folders of the project that hold WAV files; the built-in sound is listed as such) and a grid with one row per voice, as wide as the steps of the block (16 without it). With the built-in sound the voices are kick, snare, hat, openhat, clap, rim, tom, lowtom, hightom and crash (no pan and tune there). A click cycles a step through rest, hit (x), accent (X), ghost note (o). Add a voice of the kit, remove one, start from a preset (beat-A, beat-B) or clear the grid; a voice without a file is struck through in red with the message the build would give. Typed number fields (with arrows, and optional sliders, see Web UI) write steps, swing and humanize; the guitar has stagger and gain.
  • Guitar: a sample set chooser (folders with note-named files), a strum row (rest, D, d, U, u, x per step), extra bars for a pattern that changes per bar, and the voicing.
  • A pattern or strum that cannot be read as a grid is not hidden: the panel says why and offers a reset; the text field stays editable.
  • The editors are disabled while the block is locked or the song has errors, like the other parameters.

Determinism

Internally a folder becomes an Instrument (a list of immutable Region records: key and velocity range, root, tune, gain, loop fields, group, sequence position, sample) and RegionResolver.Pick / PickVoice choose the region for a note or voice, velocity and counter. Drums, guitar, piano and bass all play through it (the guitar shares the nearest-note code of piano and bass). One file is one region, so sound and bytes are unchanged.

All of it is integer arithmetic: the same files, the same song and the same seed give the same samples on every machine (the pitch ratios come from the decimal twelfth root of two, not from floating-point maths). The renderers say so in their toolprint (ample-sampler).

Words from a file

A lyrics block names a file with file lyrics/song.lyr. When that file exists and is not empty, its lines are the words (without the [bar N] markers); otherwise the text parameter is used (lines separated by /). The hash of the file is part of the plan, so editing the words in the lyrics editor makes the voice a new take, and the web UI marks the build as out of date through GET /api/doc/inputs.

Not built

  • No audition of single samples and no waveform view in the UI yet: sets are folders on disk, and the step editors only write the text parameters.
  • Sample sets are looked up in the project only (not in linked folders or packs yet).
  • The demo packs still hold one hit per note (the mf round robin 1 and the vl8 hits); layers and round robins are for packs that bring them.
  • The bass and piano blocks still synthesise; a sampled piano is the same as the guitar block with another set.
  • SFZ reading (see "SFZ sets" above) does not yet cover release-triggered samples, filter modulation/envelope, LFOs or <curve> blocks; plan/sfz-import/README.md tracks the remaining work.

Building a set with the assistant (2026-10-20)

The assistant can make a sample set itself. Plan: plan/sample-set-assistant/README.md.

  • ample_sample_set_add turns an audio file into one WAV of a set: source is a project audio file, or workspace/<path> for a fetched preview (mp3, flac, ogg, aiff, m4a; decoded to WAV with ffmpeg), destination a new .wav inside the set folder named by note (samples/campfire/c4.wav; a layer is c4_v2_r1.wav). It never overwrites and changes only the staged proposal.
  • loop: true finds loop points for that sample and writes them into the folder's set.json under its base name (a layer loops under the same name). The search is deterministic: the loop starts after the attack (20 to 50 percent of the sample), ends in the tail (55 to 95 percent), and the pair whose ~10 ms of audio before the end best matches the audio before the start wins (normalised correlation times how alike the energy is); both points move to the nearest rising zero crossing and the crossfade is ~5 ms. The answer carries start, end, crossfade and a quality (near 1 is a clean loop). A sample under a quarter of a second, or with no matching stretch, gets found: false and plays as a one-shot (right for a pluck). The points are written as plain numbers: a build never depends on the finder.
  • envelope writes one ADSR for the whole set (attack, hold, decay and release in ms, sustain 0-100) next to the loops; a later call keeps the loops already there.
  • The block or channel then plays the folder with set=samples/campfire (a drums block with kit=). No .sf2 is written (a set is a folder, hashed into the plan like any sample).

The sequencer block

Status (2026-10-08): built (plan fl-block). An advanced block: the node editor and the source stay the main ways to work.

A sequencer block is a small studio in one block: channels (the sounds), patterns (what each channel plays), a playlist (which patterns play when) and lanes (extra outputs that carry the channels you pick). Everything is text, in a project file sequences/.seq that the block names with file.

sequencer sq at 1 for 8 {
  file sequences/groove.seq
  lanes lane1=kick+hat lane2=bass lane3=lead
}

The file

sequencer 1
channel kick drum sample=samples/kit/kick.wav vol=-2 color=#e8505b
channel bass bass vol=-6
channel lead notes wave=triangle set=samples/felt shift=0
channel pad loop file=samples/loops/pad.wav bars=2
pattern verse bars=2 color=#4a90d9
  kick x...x...x...x...|x...x...x..xx...
  bass 1:0:1:45:100 2:0:2:43:100
  lead 1:0:1:69:96 1:1:1:72:96
  pad on
playlist
  clip verse track=1 at=1 for=4
  section Verse at=1 for=4 color=#4a90d9
  • Channel types: drum (a WAV file and steps), loop (an audio file that starts every bars bars), notes, bass and piano (the compact notes of the piano roll, played by a built-in tone, wave=square|triangle|saw, or by a sample set, set=samples/folder; shift moves the pitch in semitones), guitar (a strum row over chords, played from a pitched sample set: set=samples/gtr voicing=open|triad|power stagger=22) and gm (notes played by a General MIDI SoundFont preset: file=pack:musescore-general or a .sf2 of the project, program=0..127, bank). Common settings: vol (dB), pan (-32 to 32), mute=on, solo=on, color.
  • Guitar row: the strum (16 steps a bar, D d U u x ., bars separated by |), then the word chords and one chord name for each bar: D...D.u.D.u.D.u. chords Am F. Chord names: C, Am, F#m, Bb, G7, Cmaj7 (minor when the name has m, otherwise major).
  • Rows of a pattern: a drum row has 16 steps a bar (x hit, X accent, o ghost, 1 to 9 velocity, . rest), bars separated by |; a shorter row repeats. A bar written with 12 characters is a bar of eighth triplets, with 24 sixteenth triplets and with 32 thirty-second notes (so x..x..x..x.. is a triplet figure); a bar may use a different grid than the next. A notes row is the text of the piano roll (bar:beat:length:pitch:velocity, the bar inside the pattern). A loop plays in a pattern that has a row for it (pad on).
  • Length: a sequencer that is placed (at 1 for 4) is as long as its placement; one that is not placed is as long as its playlist (the end of the last clip), not 8 bars.
  • Playlist: a clip puts a pattern at a bar for a number of bars; when the clip is longer than the pattern the pattern repeats. A section is a named band and a marker (marker Drop at=9) a named flag: neither changes the sound. A loop (loop at=1 for=4) makes the bars from its start on play the loop bars again and again, to the end of the block.
  • Variations: pattern verse-b from=verse starts with the rows and the length of verse; its own rows replace the row of the same channel, and a row that is just - silences that channel. A variation starts from a plain pattern (one level); in the workspace the Variation button makes one and an inherited row is drawn lighter.
  • Lines starting with # are comments: they stay above the line that follows them (and at the very top and end of the file) when the editor writes the file, and go away with that line when you delete it; blank lines are not kept. Mistakes are AMP5380 with the line.

Lanes

The block has the output mix (every channel) and lane1 to lane8. lanes lane1=kick+hat lane2=bass lane3=all says which channels each lane carries (channels joined by +, all for every channel). Only lanes that name channels come out; connecting a lane that carries nothing stops the block that reads it (AMP5251) instead of silently giving the mix. Change what a lane carries by changing one line. A lane can be rendered to a file on its own.

The workspace

Select the block and press Open the sequencer (or use the block menu). The channel rack lists the channels with colour, type, mute, solo, level, pan and the sample, loop or tone; the pattern tabs hold the patterns (New, Duplicate, Rename, Delete, bars, colour) with a step grid for each drum channel, a Piano roll for notes channels and a switch for loops; the playlist has tracks with clips (click an empty spot to put the selected pattern there, drag to move, drag the right edge to resize, Delete removes) and section bands; the lanes strip has a chip per channel for each lane and Render to file per lane. Apply and back writes the file; Undo and back leaves it as it was; the save control and Ctrl+S work as everywhere. Recording into a channel is the piano roll's MIDI in.

Playing in the workspace

The bar has a transport: Play (builds first when the file changed), Stop, Repeat (keep looping) and Live. Drag over the ruler of the playlist to choose the bars that repeat (a shaded band; the ✕ next to the label clears it), click a bar to start from there (also while it plays), press ⟳ on a section band to repeat that section, or ⟳ Play pattern next to the pattern tabs to repeat the first place of that pattern. The playhead runs over the playlist. The loop plays through an audio element (web/app/loopplayer.js) and jumps back within a few milliseconds. With Live on, a change made while it plays is built in the background after a short pause and the new take replaces the old one exactly when the loop comes round again, never in the middle of a bar. This is render-and-swap, not synthesis in the browser. Closing with Undo and back puts the file back as it was before the live builds wrote it.

Keeping the sequence in the song

The sequence can live in the song itself instead of a file: a sequence { ... } part of the block holds the text of a sequence file (every line indented two more than sequence {; the closing brace stands at the indent of the opening line):

sequencer band at 1 for 8 {
  lanes lane1=kick
  sequence {
    sequencer 1
    channel kick drum sample=samples/kick.wav
    pattern verse bars=2
      kick x...x...x...x...|x...x...x...x...
    playlist
      clip verse track=1 at=1 for=8
  }
}

It is used instead of file. In the sequencer workspace Keep in the song moves the sequence of the file into the block (the file stays where it is, the block just stops using it) and Extract to a file… writes it to a new .ampleseq file of the project and lets the block use that file again. The workspace opens and writes a sequence in the song the same way as a file. New sequence files get the extension .ampleseq; a .seq file of before still works.

Not built yet

Automation clips on the playlist, time-stretched loops (a loop plays at its own speed), playback markers that start playing at a point (the loop range is built).

Score import: from a MIDI, MusicXML, MuseScore/Guitar Pro or PDF/image score to a sequence

Status (2026-10-15): built (tool ample_import_score). For the assistant and for people.

A score that exists as MIDI (.mid) or MusicXML (.musicxml, .xml, or zipped as .mxl) becomes a sequence file that AMPLE can play and edit, without a conversion script. A MuseScore, Guitar Pro, Capella or Overture file (.mscz, .mscx, .gp, .gp3-.gp5, .gpx, .ptb, .ove, .cap, .capx, .bww) is converted to MusicXML with MuseScore when it is installed - see "MuseScore/Guitar Pro/Capella/Overture files" below. A score that only exists as a PDF or image (.pdf, .png, .jpg, .jpeg, .webp, .tif, .tiff) is recognized first with Audiveris (optical music recognition, OMR) when it is installed - see "PDF and image scores (OMR)" below.

What you get

ample_import_score { path, out?, bars_per_pattern? } writes a new .ampleseq in the proposal:

  • one channel per part: channel violin1 gm file=pack:musescore-general program=40 bank=0 vol=-6 pan=0 (the General MIDI program of the part is kept; a drum channel uses bank 128);
  • the notes as rows bar:beat:length:pitch:velocity in patterns of bars_per_pattern bars (default 8), named part-1, part-9, ...;
  • a playlist that plays the patterns in order (clip part-1 track=1 at=1 for=8). The answer says how many parts, notes and bars there are, the tempo of the score (set the project tempo to it) and warnings for what could not be kept.

A MIDI file in pieces, with the sound of the file (2026-10-28)

The import of a MIDI file keeps what the MIDI renderer plays, in pieces of bars_per_pattern bars:

  • Exact ticks: the channel line has ppq=480 (the ticks of the file) and the rows are bar:tick:length-in-ticks:pitch:velocity; a note that goes over a bar line is cut there and its pieces share ;tie=N, so it plays as one note. A short drum gate keeps its real length.
  • Controllers and pitch bends: a row <channel>.events in each pattern holds them as bar:tick:c|p:data1:data2 (c = controller such as 7 volume, 11 expression, 64 sustain, 10 pan; p = pitch bend with its two seven-bit bytes). The soundfont renderer plays them with the notes.
  • Tempo changes: the notes and events are put at their real time at the first tempo (ppq grows to the unit that makes every tick a whole number, for example 960 when a part runs at twice the first tempo), so the sound is right and the bars of the sequence are those of the first tempo.
  • Level: a channel is imported with vol=-6 (thirteen parts at 0 dB clip, the MIDI renderer has a soft limiter that the sequencer has not). Set vol=0 when you want the level of the MIDI block.

Checked on a 13-part MIDI (2026-10-28): the sequence and the midi-render of the same file are equal to 1 unit of 16 bits in the stretch without tempo changes (the sequencer is stereo, so a centred channel is 3 dB lower on one side: the pan law); where the tempo changes, both start every note at the same moment, the sequence to the sample and the MIDI renderer to the tick (1/480 beat), so the waveforms differ in phase and not in energy.

Short. A pattern that says exactly what an earlier one says is not written again (the playlist plays the earlier one) and a pattern that shares most rows with an earlier one is a variation (from=) that lists only what differs. With compress=true a row is written as a formula (a rhythm that repeats with pitches and velocities that cycle, docs/language/17-note-completeness-and-formulas.md) when that is at least 40 percent shorter and was checked to give the very same notes.

What it keeps and what it does not

Kept Not kept (a warning says so)
Parts and their program, pitches, start and length in beats, ties (joined), chords, rests, simple repeats (a backward repeat jumps back once) Time signatures other than 4/4 (a bar here is four beats), tempo changes (the first tempo is used), MIDI controllers that the soundfont renderer does not play (all controllers are kept in the events row, the renderer plays 7, 11, 10, 64 and the pitch bend), first and second endings (played in written order), dynamics (all notes at velocity 90 for MusicXML, the written velocity for MIDI), grace notes, ornaments and articulation

How to use it in a song

  1. Put the score file in the project (or fetch it with ample_fetch_url; Mutopia and similar sites offer MIDI and MusicXML).
  2. ample_import_score { path: "scores/k525.mid", out: "sequences/k525.ampleseq" }.
  3. Add a sequencer block that names the file and give it lanes for the sounds you want to treat separately:
    sequencer score {
  file sequences/k525.ampleseq
  lanes lane1=violin1+violin2 lane2=viola lane3=cello+bass
}
  4. Set the project tempo to the tempo from the answer. A song is as long as the playlist; a part may reach bar 1024.
  5. Change instruments, volumes and lanes in the sequence; make it sound the way the song needs (see sequencer).

MuseScore/Guitar Pro/Capella/Overture files

When path ends in one of MuseScore's own read formats, AMPLE runs MuseScore (<file> -o <file>.musicxml) and imports the result - this is a straight, machine conversion of the file's own note data (not recognition), so it is as reliable as the source file:

  • Install MuseScore (not bundled with AMPLE): the official installer works; a portable build (its .paf.exe accepts /S for a silent self-extraction next to itself, or use the PortableApps.com build) needs no admin rights. Set AMPLE_MUSESCORE to the resulting MuseScore4.exe, or put it on the PATH. ample doctor --env reports whether it is found.
  • A .mxl (zipped MusicXML) needs neither Audiveris nor MuseScore: AMPLE unzips it directly.

PDF and image scores (OMR)

When path ends in .pdf, .png, .jpg, .jpeg, .webp, .tif or .tiff, AMPLE runs Audiveris on it in batch mode and imports the MusicXML it recognizes:

  • Install Audiveris (not bundled with AMPLE): its Windows installer needs admin rights for a normal install; without them, extract it per-user with msiexec /a Audiveris-x.y.z-windowsConsole-x86_64.msi /quiet TARGETDIR="<a short path>" (a long TARGETDIR can fail with "Error writing to file" - Audiveris's own class files have long names). Set AMPLE_AUDIVERIS to the resulting Audiveris.exe, or put it on the PATH. ample doctor --env reports whether it is found.
  • It can be wrong. OMR reads printed symbols, not music: a scanned or low-quality source, unusual notation, or a lot of text can come out with missing, extra or mis-pitched notes. The answer's next note says to check the result; always look at the note count and a few bars against the source before trusting it.
  • Getting a PDF into the project first: a score fetched from the web lands outside ./project (ample_fetch_url's assets/web/); stage it into the project with ample_copy_file (source: "workspace/assets/web/<file>") before importing it.
  • Large or dense scores can take a few minutes; Audiveris is stopped after 3 minutes with a timeout message if it has not finished.

Tips

  • Long scores: more bars_per_pattern makes fewer, longer patterns; fewer makes it easier to rearrange sections.
  • The import never overwrites a file: give another out or change the file with ample_edit.
